In 1955, Hugh Ross Williamson argued that the Man in the Iron Mask was the natural father of Louis XIV. According to this theory, the "miraculous" birth of Louis XIV in 1638 would have come after Louis XIII had been estranged from his wife Anne of Austria for 14 years.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002245-249)

The theory then suggests that Cardinal Richelieu had arranged for a substitute, probably an illegitimate grandson of [Henry IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_France "Henry IV of France"),[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002247-250) to become intimate with the Queen and father an heir in the King's stead. At the time, the [heir presumptive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heir_presumptive "Heir presumptive") was Louis XIII's brother [Gaston, Duke of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaston,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Gaston, Duke of Orléans"), who was Richelieu's enemy. If Gaston became king, Richelieu would quite likely have lost both his job as minister and his life, and so it was in his best interests to thwart Gaston's ambitions.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002246-251)

Supposedly, the substitute father then left for the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_France "New France") but returned to France in the 1660s with the aim of extorting money for keeping his secret and was promptly imprisoned. This theory would explain the secrecy surrounding the prisoner, whose true identity would have destroyed the legitimacy of Louis XIV's claim to the throne had it been revealed.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002247%E2%80%93248-252)

This theory had been suggested by British politician [Hugh Cecil, 1st Baron Quickswood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Cecil,_1st_Baron_Quickswood "Hugh Cecil, 1st Baron Quickswood"), who nonetheless added that the idea has no historical basis and is entirely hypothetical.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002245-249) Williamson held that: "to say it is a guess with no solid historical basis is merely to say that it is like every other theory on the matter, although it makes more sense than any of the other theories. There is no known evidence that is incompatible with it, even the age of the prisoner, which Cecil had considered a weak point;[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002249%E2%80%93251-253) and it explains every aspect of the mystery."[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002245-249) His time spent as a valet to another prisoner renders this idea doubtful, however.[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-valet-67)

#### Philippe d'Orléans's younger brother

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Philippe d'Orléans's younger brother")]

In 2024, Canadian author Sarah B. Madry claimed that, in January 1666, Louis XIV received his mother's confession on her deathbed that he was a child of François d'Auger de Cavoye, the captain of Cardinal Richelieu's personal guards, and his wife Marie de Cavoye. This theory aligns with historical speculation that a surrogate was arranged by Anne of Austria to answer the French state's peril of the lack of an heir for her dying husband King Louis XIII and to seek revenge at what she perceived as abuse for many years by her husband and Cardinal Richelieu. According to Madry's theory, the man in the iron mask was a younger brother of [Philippe I, Duke of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_I,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Philippe I, Duke of Orléans"), and that this "second son" of Louis XIII and Anne of Austria was born in October or November 1643. The child was never presented or acknowledged because of a facial genetic defect, and was therefore assigned to caretakers under the name of "Eustache Dauger". In 1669, Louis XIV ordered his imprisonment, lest the disfigured man might one day claim the throne.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMadry2024-254)

### Italian diplomat

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Italian diplomat")]

Another candidate, much favoured in the 1800s, was Count Ercole Antonio Mattioli (a.k.a. Matthioli). He was an Italian diplomat who acted on behalf of the debt-ridden [Charles IV, Duke of Mantua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_IV,_Duke_of_Mantua "Charles IV, Duke of Mantua") in 1678, in selling [Casale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casale_Monferrato "Casale Monferrato"), a strategic fortified town near the border with France. A French occupation would be unpopular, so discretion was essential, but Mattioli leaked the details to France's Spanish enemies after pocketing his commission once the sale had been concluded, and they made a bid of their own before the French forces could occupy the town. At the end of April 1679, Mattioli was lured onto French soil near Turin, where he was kidnapped by a French team of two officers and four soldiers under the command of Nicolas Catinat, and incarcerated into nearby Pignerol on 2 May.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196166%E2%80%9373-57) The French took possession of Casale two years later.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988-59)

[George Agar-Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Agar-Ellis "George Agar-Ellis") reached the conclusion that Mattioli was the Man in the Iron Mask when he reviewed documents extracted from French archives in the 1820s.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAgar-Ellis1826-255) His book, published in English in 1826, was translated into French and published in 1830. German historian Wilhelm Broecking came to the same conclusion independently seventy years later. [Robert Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Chambers_(journalist) "Robert Chambers (journalist)")' _[Book of Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chambers\_Book\_of\_Days "Chambers Book of Days")_ supports the claim and places Mattioli in the Bastille for the last 13 years of his life. The **Man in the Iron Mask** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _L'Homme au Masque de Fer_; died 19 November 1703) was an unidentified prisoner of state during the reign of [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV "Louis XIV") of France (1643–1715). The strict measures taken to keep his imprisonment secret resulted in a long-lasting legend about his identity. Warranted for arrest on 19 July 1669 under the name of "Eustache Dauger", he was apprehended near [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais") on 28 July, incarcerated on 24 August, and held for 34 years in the custody of [Bénigne Dauvergne de Saint-Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9nigne_Dauvergne_de_Saint-Mars "Bénigne Dauvergne de Saint-Mars") in four successive French prisons, including the [Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille "Bastille"). He died there on 19 November 1703, and his burial certificate bore the name of "Marchioly", leading several historians to conclude that the prisoner was Italian diplomat [Ercole Antonio Mattioli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Antonio_Mattioli "Ercole Antonio Mattioli").

His true identity remains a mystery, even though it has been extensively debated by historians, and various theories have been expounded in numerous books, articles, poems, plays, and films. During his lifetime, it was rumoured that he was a [Marshal of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshal_of_France#Louis_XIV,_1643%E2%80%931715 "Marshal of France") or a President of _[Parlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlement#The\_Fronde "Parlement")_, the [Duke of Beaufort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois,_Duke_of_Beaufort "François, Duke of Beaufort"), or a son of [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"), and some of these rumours were initiated by Saint-Mars himself. Among the oldest theories is one proposed by French philosopher and writer [Voltaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire "Voltaire"), who claimed in his _Questions sur l'Encyclopédie_ (1771) that the prisoner was an older, illegitimate brother of Louis XIV. Other writers believed that he was the King's twin or younger brother. In all, more than 50 candidates, real and hypothetical, have been proposed by historians and other authors aiming to solve the mystery.

What little is known about the prisoner is based on contemporaneous documents uncovered during the 19th century, mainly some of the correspondence between Saint-Mars and his superiors in Paris, initially [Louvois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois-Michel_le_Tellier,_Marquis_de_Louvois "François-Michel le Tellier, Marquis de Louvois"), Louis XIV's secretary of state for war. These documents show that the prisoner was labelled "only a valet" and that he was jailed for "what he was employed to do" before his arrest, and for "what he knew." Legend has it that no one ever saw his face, as it was hidden by a mask of black velvet cloth, later misreported by Voltaire as an iron mask. Official documents reveal, however, that the prisoner was made to cover his face only when travelling between prisons after 1687, or when going to prayers within the Bastille in the final years of his incarceration; modern historians believe that the measure was imposed by Saint-Mars solely to increase his own prestige, thus causing persistent rumours to circulate about this seemingly important prisoner.

In 1932, French historian Maurice Duvivier proposed that the prisoner was Eustache Dauger de Cavoye, a nobleman associated with several political scandals of the late 17th century. This solution, however, was disproved in 1953 when previously unpublished family letters were discovered by French historian [Georges Mongrédien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Mongr%C3%A9dien?action=edit&redlink=1 "Georges Mongrédien (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges%20Mongr%C3%A9dien "fr:Georges Mongrédien")], who concluded that the enigma remained unsolved.

He has been the subject of many works of fiction, most prominently [Alexandre Dumas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Dumas "Alexandre Dumas")' 1850 novel _[The Vicomte of Bragelonne: Ten Years Later](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Vicomte\_of\_Bragelonne:\_Ten\_Years\_Later "The Vicomte of Bragelonne: Ten Years Later")_—the final installment of his [D'Artagnan saga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D'Artagnan_Romances "D'Artagnan Romances")—which portrays the prisoner as Louis XIV's identical twin. In 1840, Dumas had first presented a review of the popular theories about the prisoner extant in his time in the chapter "L'homme au masque de fer," published in the eighth volume of his non-fiction _Crimes Célèbres_. This approach was adopted by many subsequent authors, and speculative works have continued to appear on the subject.

## The prisoner "whose name is not spoken"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: The prisoner \"whose name is not spoken\"")]

### Arrest and imprisonment – Pignerol (1669–1681)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Arrest and imprisonment – Pignerol (1669–1681)")]

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Citadelle_de_Pignerol.jpg/250px-Citadelle_de_Pignerol.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Citadelle_de_Pignerol.jpg)

Etching of the citadel and dungeon of Pignerol, in Piedmont, Italy (c. 1650)

The earliest surviving records of the masked prisoner are from 19 July 1669,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961181-1) when [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV "Louis XIV")'s minister, the [Marquis de Louvois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois-Michel_le_Tellier,_Marquis_de_Louvois "François-Michel le Tellier, Marquis de Louvois"), sent a letter to [Bénigne Dauvergne de Saint-Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9nigne_Dauvergne_de_Saint-Mars "Bénigne Dauvergne de Saint-Mars"), governor of the prison of [Pignerol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pignerol "Pignerol") (which at the time was part of France). In his letter, Louvois informed Saint-Mars that a prisoner named "Eustache Dauger" was due to arrive in the next month or so.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961181-1)

He instructed Saint-Mars to prepare a cell with multiple doors, one closing upon the other, which were to prevent anyone from the outside listening in.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-nomask-6) Saint-Mars was to see Dauger only once a day to provide food and whatever else he needed. Dauger was to be told that if he ever spoke of anything other than his immediate needs he would be killed, but, according to Louvois, the prisoner should not require much since he was "only a valet".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961181%E2%80%93182-7) Historians have noted that the name "Eustache Dauger" was written in a handwriting different from that used in the rest of the letter's text, suggesting that a clerk wrote the letter under Louvois' dictation, while someone else, very likely Louvois, added the name afterward.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTELincoln_''Timewatch'',_1988-8)

Dauger was arrested on 28 July by Captain Alexandre de Vauroy, garrison commander of [Dunkerque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkirk "Dunkirk"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961184-9) and a small escort of three soldiers,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004111%E2%80%93112-10) who took him to Pignerol, where he arrived on 24 August.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961185-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988152-12) Evidence has been produced to suggest that the arrest was actually made in [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais") and that not even the local governor was informed of the event—Vauroy's absence being explained away by his hunting for Spanish soldiers who had strayed into France via the [Spanish Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Netherlands "Spanish Netherlands").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988151-13) The first rumours of the prisoner's identity (specifically as a [Marshal of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshal_of_France "Marshal of France")) began to circulate at this point.

#### Saint-Mars's other prisoners

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Saint-Mars's other prisoners")]

The [dungeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dungeon "Dungeon") at Pignerol was used to incarcerate men who had displeased Louis XIV or were considered an embarrassment to the state, and it usually held only a few important prisoners at a time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTELincoln_''Timewatch'',_1988-8)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-otherpris-17)

*   Saint-Mars's first prisoner of state at Pignerol was [Nicolas Fouquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Fouquet "Nicolas Fouquet"), Marquis of Belle-Île, a former [superintendent of finances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintendent_of_Finances "Superintendent of Finances") who had been arrested on 5 September 1661[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198857-18) and tried by order of Louis XIV on the charge of embezzlement.[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-fouquet-28) On 27 December 1664,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTELair1890409-27) after a long trial, Fouquet was transferred—by [d'Artagnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D'Artagnan "D'Artagnan") leading a company of 100 musketeers—from the Bastille to Pignerol, where he arrived on 16 January 1665[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTELair1890414-29) and was lodged in the Angle Tower.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988289-30)

In 1665, Saint-Mars commanded a new _compagnie franche_,[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-freecompany-33) created solely to guard Fouquet, which comprised four officers (including three musketeers detached from their original corps), 11 non-commissioned officers and 50 soldiers.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200440-34)
*   Two years after Dauger's arrival in August 1669, Saint-Mars's third prisoner was the [Marquis de Lauzun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Nompar_de_Caumont "Antoine Nompar de Caumont"), a favourite of Louis XIV, who had fallen from grace for lying to the King and insulting his mistress, [Madame de Montespan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madame_de_Montespan "Madame de Montespan").[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-lauzun-41)[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-lauzun2-52) For this, Lauzun was arrested on 25 November 1671[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2015149-53) and, with an escort of 100 musketeers led once again by d'Artagnan,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2015150-54) was brought to Pignerol on 16 December of that year, and lodged in rooms directly under Fouquet's cell.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988155-42)

At that time, the strength of Saint-Mars's company was increased from 65 to 135 men, officers included.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200441-48)
*   A [Dominican monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_monk "Dominican monk"), nicknamed Lapierre, was brought to Pignerol on 7 April 1674. He was a swindler, dabbling in [alchemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemy "Alchemy"), who had abused the trust of several ladies at court, including the wife of [Louis de Lorraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis,_Count_of_Armagnac "Louis, Count of Armagnac"), one of the [Great Officers of the Crown of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Officers_of_the_Crown_of_France "Great Officers of the Crown of France") and a member of the [King's Household](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maison_du_Roi "Maison du Roi"). Soon after his incarceration, Lapierre became insane, screaming hysterically, fouling his cell, and insulting his guards.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200445-55)

*   In May 1676, Saint-Mars received a fifth prisoner, named Dubreuil, a private agent specialising in military espionage, who was discovered to be in the pay of the Austrian and Spanish governments as well as the French. Louvois had ordered his kidnapping on 25 February and Dubreuil was caught on 24 April.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988162%E2%80%93163-56)

*   Another prisoner was Count [Ercole Antonio Mattioli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercole_Antonio_Mattioli "Ercole Antonio Mattioli"), an Italian diplomat who had double-crossed Louis XIV over the purchase of the important fortress town of [Casale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casale_Monferrato "Casale Monferrato") on the [Mantuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Mantua "Duchy of Mantua") border. Mattioli was kidnapped near [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin") by a small team of French soldiers commanded by [Nicolas Catinat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Catinat "Nicolas Catinat"), and incarcerated at Pignerol on 2 May 1679.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196166%E2%80%9373-57) Mattioli's Italian valet, named Rousseau, was also arrested and taken to Pignerol two days later. (French historian Jean-Christian Petitfils suggested that "Rousseau" might have been a francisation of the name "Rosso").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200446%E2%80%9347-58)

#### Dauger serves as a valet (1675–1680)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Dauger serves as a valet (1675–1680)")]

In his letters to Louvois, Saint-Mars describes Dauger as a quiet man, giving no trouble, "disposed to the will of God and to the King", compared to his other prisoners, who were always complaining, constantly trying to escape, or simply mad.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988-59) Dauger was not always isolated from the other prisoners. Wealthy and important ones usually had manservants; for instance, Fouquet was granted the service of two men in 1667, called Champagne and La Rivière,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961187-60)[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-lariviere-63) and Mattioli had been joined by his Italian valet, Rousseau, incarcerated with him in 1679. These servants, however, would become as much prisoners as their masters and it was thus difficult to find people willing to volunteer for such an occupation. When Lauzun arrived in December 1671, Saint-Mars could not find him a manservant, and therefore wrote to Louvois on 20 February 1672, suggesting that Dauger would prove a good valet for Lauzun. This request was turned down, and historians believe Louvois had reasons to keep these two men apart; perhaps they knew each other.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961187%E2%80%93188-64)

In 1674, Champagne died and, since La Rivière was often ill, Saint-Mars again applied for permission for Dauger to act as servant, this time for Fouquet.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961188-65) On 30 January 1675, Louvois gave permission for such an arrangement on strict condition that he was to serve Fouquet only while La Rivière was unavailable and that he was not to meet anyone else; for instance, if Fouquet and Lauzun were to meet, Dauger was not to be present. This injunction was reiterated by Louvois to Saint-Mars in a stern letter dated 11 March 1675. Fouquet was never expected to be released; thus, meeting Dauger was no great matter, but Lauzun was expected to be set free eventually, and it would have been important not to have him spread rumours of Dauger's existence or of secrets he might have known. Shortly thereafter, Dauger was moved from the Lower Tower to the Angle Tower, where he was lodged with La Rivière.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961189-66) The important fact that Dauger served as a valet to Fouquet strongly indicates he was born a [commoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commoner "Commoner").[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-valet-67)

On 23 November 1678, Louvois wrote directly to Fouquet to inform him that the King was disposed to soften considerably the strictures of his incarceration, subject to Fouquet writing back to Louvois—without informing Saint-Mars of the contents of his reply—concerning whether or not Dauger had talked to him, Fouquet, in front of La Rivière, "about what he was employed to do before being brought to Pignerol".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961190-68) From this revealing letter, French historian Mongrédien concluded that Louvois was clearly anxious that any details about Dauger's former employment should not leak out if the King decided to relax the conditions of Fouquet's or Lauzun's incarceration.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961191-69)

After Fouquet's death on 23 March 1680, Saint-Mars discovered a secret hole between Fouquet and Lauzun's cells.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTESandars1909390%E2%80%93392-70) He was sure that they had communicated through this hole without detection by him or his guards and thus that Lauzun must have been made aware of Dauger's existence.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961192%E2%80%93193-71) On 8 April 1680, Louvois therefore wrote to Saint-Mars and instructed him to move Lauzun to Fouquet's cell and to tell him that Dauger and La Rivière had been released, after secretly relocating them to a new cell in the Lower Tower of Pignerol's dungeon.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961193-72)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTELincoln_''Timewatch'',_1988-8) They became henceforth identified in official correspondence only as "the gentlemen of the lower tower" ("les messieurs de la tour d'en bas").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961195%E2%80%93196-73) After Fouquet's death, the strength of Saint-Mars's company was decreased from 135 to 65 men, officers included.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200441-48)

Lauzun was freed a year later, on 22 April 1681.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988173-74) The King put him under the constant guard of Maupertuis[[i]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-maupertuis-76)—a lieutenant of musketeers and friend of Saint-Mars—and 12 musketeers,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTESandars1909429-77) and ordered that he should be taken to [Bourbon-l'Archambault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourbon-l'Archambault "Bourbon-l'Archambault") for a cure, then assigned a residence in [Chalon-sur-Saône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalon-sur-Sa%C3%B4ne "Chalon-sur-Saône"), and finally begin his rehabilitation at [Amboise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amboise "Amboise").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200441-48) The King consented to see him once and, after the interview, he was allowed to go wherever he pleased, including Paris, but was banned from attending court in Versailles.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTESandars1909437,_444-78) The King also informed his cousin, the Duchess of Montpensier, that he would never consent to her marriage with Lauzun.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPagnol197379-79)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTESandars1909424-80) Lauzun's release from Pignerol marked the end of Saint-Mars's custody of prestigious prisoners, and his company was reduced from 65 to 45 men, officers included.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200452-81)

### Subsequent prisons (1681–1703)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Subsequent prisons (1681–1703)")]

#### Exilles (1681–1687)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Exilles (1681–1687)")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Exilles02.JPG/250px-Exilles02.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Exilles02.JPG)

[Fortress of Exilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortress_of_Exilles "Fortress of Exilles")

With the impending acquisition of the town of [Casale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casale_Monferrato "Casale Monferrato") by France, finally resolved despite Mattioli's treachery, the concentration of French troops around Pignerol required extensive works to be carried out at the citadel. Louvois therefore decided to transfer Dauger and La Rivière, "the two most important prisoners", to the fortress of [Exilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exilles_Fort "Exilles Fort"), located about 40 km (25 mi) west of Pignerol, on the road to [Briançon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian%C3%A7on "Briançon"), and appointed Saint-Mars as its governor on 12 May 1681,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196189%E2%80%9390-82)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988291-83) with an income of 2,000 _[livres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French\_livre "French livre")_ per annum.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196193-84)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPagnol1973202-85)[[j]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-smpayexilles-89)[[k]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-cut-91) The other three prisoners, Dubreuil, Lapierre, and Mattioli (plus his valet, Rousseau) all remained at Pignerol.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196193-84)Saint-Mars's company of 45 men,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196193%E2%80%9394-92) including two lieutenants,[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200455-93) was deemed necessary to protect the fortress from being raided by a force intent on liberating the two valets,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200452-81) although a more likely reason was that Louvois wanted to save his protégé from loss of income and prestige, and from perceiving his move to Exilles as a fall from grace.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200452-81)

Since the prison in Exilles also needed modifications, including to secure the cell of the two prisoners with the same multiple doors as had been constructed at Pignerol, the transfer of prisoners was postponed until the works were completed.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196193-84) An additional delay, requiring Saint-Mars's diligent attention a little longer at Pignerol, was caused by the final negotiations of the transfer of Casale to France, during which Nicolas Catinat had been secretly lodged at Pignerol under the pseudonym of "Guibert",[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196197%E2%80%9398-94) prior to his troops' successful occupation of Casale, to which he was appointed governor on 1 October.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961100%E2%80%93101-95)

Shortly thereafter, Saint-Mars and his free company finally undertook the short journey to Exilles, with Dauger and La Rivière transported in a [horse-drawn litter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litter_(vehicle) "Litter (vehicle)") curtained by leather or oilcloth, as instructed by Louvois in his letter on 9 June.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961103-96)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988255%E2%80%93256-97)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200457-98)

After the intense daily routine of Pignerol and its troublesome prisoners, Saint-Mars found Exilles to be a much quieter posting, isolated, sad and boring. He never missed an opportunity to absent himself, by going hunting, walking in nearby valleys, or visiting his friend Jean-Jacques Losa, governor of [Susa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susa,_Piedmont "Susa, Piedmont") for the Duke of Savoy, [Victor Amadeus II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Amadeus_II "Victor Amadeus II").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200455-93) He regularly wrote requests to take more leave, which Louvois and the King often declined to grant him.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200456-99) His two prisoners were still being kept under extraordinarily strict precautions for mere valets, while Louvois seemed to care little for the three left at Pignerol.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200456-99) In a letter dated 2 March 1682, he wrote to Saint-Mars:

> The King ordered me to instruct you to have them guarded so severely that you could assure His Majesty that they would speak to nobody whatsoever, not only from without but also from within the Exilles garrison itself. I request that you inform me from time to time about what happens concerning them.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200456-99)

On 11 March, Saint-Mars replied:

> My prisoners are guarded day and night by two soldiers posted on both sides of the tower, looking obliquely at the prisoners' windows, with instructions to listen if anyone speaks to them, or if they shout from their windows, and to hurry away any passers-by who stopped along the path or on the slope of the mountain. Inside the tower, I have divided it in such a way that the priest delivering mass can't see them, thanks to a [tambour door](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambour_door "Tambour door") that was installed at my request to cover their multiple doors. The servants who bring their food place the necessary on a table outside their cell, and my lieutenant takes it and brings it to them. Nobody speaks to them, save myself, my officer [lieutenant La Prade], the priest [the abbé Antoine Rignon] and a doctor from [Pragelato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pragelato "Pragelato"), six [leagues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_(unit)#France "League (unit)") away, and in my presence only. For their clothes, same precautions I applied for my prisoners in the past.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200456%E2%80%9357-100)

To which Louvois replied, on 31 March: "The King does not want that another lieutenant than the one accustomed to speak to them has any communications with them whatsoever."[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200457-98) After the abbé Rignon died, Louvois wrote to Saint-Mars on 3 June 1682: "Your prisoners should only be confessed following an order from the King or when in peril of imminent death, and this you will observe, if you please."[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200458-101) When Saint-Mars, now approaching the age of 60, requested some leave to go and take the waters at [Aix-les-Bains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aix-les-Bains "Aix-les-Bains"), Louvois responded, on 7 March 1685:

> The King desires that you go and take some fresh air wherever you deem suitable to your health, but His Majesty recommends that you give such good orders for your prisoners' security that nobody could have communications with them while you are absent, and that there will be no misadventure."[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200459-102)

During their imprisonment at Exilles, the two prisoners were often ill[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961103-96) and, in June 1685, La Rivière asked permission to make his will.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961112-103) In October 1686, he became seriously ill with [dropsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropsy "Dropsy")[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961113-104) and died in early January 1687.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961115-105) His death-bed confession was probably heard by the abbé Guy Favre, appointed in May 1686 to provide religious services to the whole company.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200459-102) After La Rivière's death, Dauger was referred to as "La Tour" by prison staff[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196125,_235-106) and as "the old prisoner" ("l'ancien prisonnier") in correspondence.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961197-61)

In Pignerol, Dubreuil had been freed on 13 June 1684, when the [Truce of Ratisbonne](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C3%AAve%20de%20Ratisbonne "fr:Trêve de Ratisbonne") stipulated the liberation of war prisoners.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200472,_269-107) He was re-arrested in June 1696 for dealing in counterfeit money between [Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyon "Lyon") and [Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva "Geneva"), and incarcerated at the [Château de Pierre Encise](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau%20de%20Pierre%20Scize "fr:Château de Pierre Scize") prison, where he died in May 1711.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200472,_273-108)

#### Île Sainte-Marguerite (1687–1698)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Île Sainte-Marguerite (1687–1698)")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Lerins-iron_mask_prison.jpg/250px-Lerins-iron_mask_prison.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lerins-iron_mask_prison.jpg)

Fort Royal in [Île Sainte-Marguerite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Ele_Sainte-Marguerite "Île Sainte-Marguerite"), showing the main door to the extension of 1687 and, on the left, the rectangular wing of four new cells added in 1690.

In January 1687, Louvois appointed Saint-Mars governor of [Île Sainte-Marguerite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Ele_Sainte-Marguerite "Île Sainte-Marguerite") and [Île Saint-Honorat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Ele_Saint-Honorat "Île Saint-Honorat"), the two largest of the [Lérins Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9rins_Islands "Lérins Islands") half a mile offshore from Cannes.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200460-109) Saint-Mars was to be based at Sainte-Marguerite's Fort Royal, along with his company of 45 men, even though the existing garrison already numbered more than 300 men.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200463-110)[[l]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-fortroyal-111)

Fort Royal was a citadel on a war footing with [bastions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastions "Bastions"), [ditches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ditch "Ditch"), [ravelins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravelin "Ravelin"), and fortified walls, but was not a real prison, with only a few rooms in the main castle sometimes used to house deserters or the wayward sons of notable families.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200463-110) After several visits to determine the works required to house his sole prisoner in the usual way, Saint-Mars decided to add another level to the castle for himself, including two new spacious cells on the ground floor,[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200463-110) increased to six in 1690 by the addition of a rectangular wing connected to the castle.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200468,_70,_240-112)

Saint-Mars and his company finally left Exilles on 17 April and arrived in Sainte-Marguerite on 30 April, after a journey of 50 leagues (200 km; 124 mi).[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200465-113) Dauger was transported in a [sedan chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litter_(vehicle)#In_Europe "Litter (vehicle)") covered by an oilcloth,[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200462-114) carried on the shoulders of four Italian porters who, in relay with four others, had taken him over mountain roads, then by main roads to Cannes.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988256,_264-115)[[m]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-stages-116)

On 3 May, Saint-Mars wrote to Louvois:

> The journey took 12 days, because my prisoner was ill and complaining that he suffered from not having enough air. I can assure you, Sir, that nobody in the world saw him, and that the way I guarded him during the whole journey caused everyone to seek to guess who my prisoner might be. [...] My prisoner's bed was so old and broken, as was everything else he used, whether table linen or furniture, that it wasn't worth bringing here, and we sold them all for only 13 _[écus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cu#Silver\_Louis\_or\_%C3%A9cu\_of\_1641 "Écu")_ (39 _livres_).[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200466-117)

On his arrival, Dauger was lodged in a small—and somewhat unsanitary—fortified shed that had been built behind the castle in 1685, until his new cell was completed in December 1687.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200464,_66-118)[[n]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-stmargcell-120) Soon thereafter, a sentinel named Aubry—who had often guarded Dauger's cell—estimated him to be about 50 years old.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004166-121)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChaudon1766252-122)[[o]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-aubry-123)

After a letter from Louvois to Saint-Mars on 5 July 1688, there is a long gap of three years in correspondence, during which nothing is known about Saint-Mars and his prisoners.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961121-124) On 16 July 1691, Louvois died and was immediately succeeded as War Minister by his son, the [Marquis of Barbezieux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Fran%C3%A7ois_Marie_Le_Tellier "Louis François Marie Le Tellier"). In his first letter to Saint-Mars, dated 13 August, Barbezieux wrote:

> Your letter of the 26th of last month has reached me. When you have something to tell me about the prisoner you have been guarding for twenty years, I ask you to use the same precautions as when you wrote to M. de Louvois.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961121-124)

This important letter, kept in the [Anciennes Archives de la Guerre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defence_Historical_Service "Defence Historical Service"),[[p]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-satarch-127) confirms that the prisoner being mentioned can only have been Eustache Dauger since, by that date, he was the only prisoner who had been kept in Saint-Mars's uninterrupted custody for 22 years, which Barbezieux approximated to "twenty years".[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961122,_197-128)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200468%E2%80%9369-129) Dauger dragged out 11 years in solitary confinement at Sainte-Marguerite, with no apparent changes, having contact with no one except Saint-Mars and his lieutenants, a doctor when he was ill, and a confessor at set times.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988268-130)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Fort_royal_de_ile_ste_marguerite.JPG/250px-Fort_royal_de_ile_ste_marguerite.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fort_royal_de_ile_ste_marguerite.JPG)

Fort Royal in [Île Sainte-Marguerite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Ele_Sainte-Marguerite "Île Sainte-Marguerite") viewed from the sea, showing windows of the six cells.

From May 1689, Saint-Mars also became answerable to the [Count of Pontchartrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Ph%C3%A9lypeaux,_Marquis_of_Ph%C3%A9lypeaux "Louis Phélypeaux, Marquis of Phélypeaux"), Louis XIV's [Controller-General of Finances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controller-General_of_Finances "Controller-General of Finances"), for six protestant ministers arrested and incarcerated at Fort Royal after the [Edict of Fontainebleau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Fontainebleau "Edict of Fontainebleau") (17 October 1685) revoked [Henry IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_France "Henry IV of France")'s [Edict of Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Nantes "Edict of Nantes") (1598). These prisoners[[q]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-protmins-132) were eventually held, sometimes several to a cell, in the rectangular wing that was appended to the castle in 1690.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988268-130)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200469%E2%80%9370,_240-131)

In Pignerol, the Dominican monk, Lapierre, died in January 1694.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200474-133) In April of that year Mattioli and his valet Rousseau were moved to Sainte-Marguerite, back into the custody of Saint-Mars; Mattioli died there on 28 April 1694,[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004261-134)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961132%E2%80%93135-135) as did Rousseau five years later, in early December 1699.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200481%E2%80%9382-136)

#### Bastille (1698–1703)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Bastille (1698–1703)")]

On 1 May 1698, Barbezieux wrote to inform Saint-Mars that Louis XIV had appointed him governor of the Bastille, the highest posting for prison officers, worth 15,168 _[livres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French\_livre "French livre")_ per annum,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961139-137)[[k]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-cut-91) plus 6,000 _livres_ in taxes levied on local shops and on boats navigating the nearby [Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine "Seine").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004163-138) Modern historians (Noone; Petitfils) pointed out that Barbezieux's letter gave no instructions concerning whether Dauger should remain at Sainte-Marguerite or be transferred to the Bastille.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988269-139)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004164-140) In a letter of 8 May, now lost, Saint-Mars must have asked for such instructions, since Barbezieux replied on 15 June:

> I have been a long time replying to the letter which you took the trouble to write to me on the 8th of last month, because the King did not inform me of his intentions sooner. You can make your dispositions to be ready to leave when I instruct you to do so, and you may bring with you your long-time prisoner under safe guard.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988269-139)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004164-140)

Noone (1988) wrote: "The fact that the King took over a month to grant his permission gives reason to believe that he did not consider the prisoner to be as important as Saint-Mars made him out to be, and this is confirmed by a letter from Barbezieux to Saint-Mars on 4 August:"[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988269-139)

> I have received the letter which you took the trouble to write to me on the 24th of last month, in which you mentioned the precautions that you must take for the transfer of your prisoner. I have conveyed these to the King, who has approved them, and sees fit that you take him with you, like I have instructed you in one of my earlier letters, that I am in no doubt you received presently. His majesty has not judged it necessary to send the order you suggested to commandeer lodging on your journey to Paris: it will suffice for you to find and pay for the most convenient and secure lodging possible in the places you decide to stay.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961141-141)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988269-139)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004165%E2%80%93166-142)

Petitfils (2004) wrote: "Instead of receiving a [safe-conduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe-conduct "Safe-conduct") enabling him to lodge without difficulty in the King's castles, military forts and citadels, Saint-Mars was instructed to organise the journey to Paris by regular roads, stopping at ordinary post-houses and hostels along the way to lodge his prisoner as best he could, and to pay his bills as he went along."[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004166-121)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988269-139)

In addition to Dauger, Saint-Mars brought with him only five members of his existing staff from Sainte-Marguerite: his nephew Guillaume de Formanoir de Corbé (lieutenant), Jacques Rosarges (major), the Abbé Honoré Giraut (chaplain), Lécuyer (sergeant/chief turnkey), and Antoine Larue, known as Rû (turnkey).[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961141%E2%80%93142-143)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988110%E2%80%93112,_269-144)[[r]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-fivestaff-146) The journey to Paris included an episode related by Guillaume-Louis Formanoir de Palteau (the son of Guillaume de Formanoir de Corbé) in a letter on 19 June 1768 to [Fréron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89lie_Catherine_Fr%C3%A9ron "Élie Catherine Fréron"), who published it at once in his _Année littéraire_:

> On his way to take up his new post, Mr. de Saint-Mars stopped off with his prisoner at his estate of [Palteau](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau%20de%20Palteau "fr:Château de Palteau"). The man with the mask arrived in a litter which preceded that of Mr. de Saint-Mars and they were accompanied by several men on horseback. The peasants went to meet their master. Mr. de Saint-Mars ate with his prisoner, whose back was turned towards the windows which gave onto the courtyard. The peasants I have questioned could not see if he had his mask on, but they saw very well that Mr. de Saint-Mars, who was facing him at the table, had two pistols beside his plate. They had only one manservant to wait on them, and the dishes were brought to an ante-chamber where he went to get them, being careful to close the door of the dining-room behind him. Whenever the prisoner crossed the courtyard he had the black mask on his face; the peasants noticed that his teeth and lips were visible, and that he was tall with white hair. Mr. de Saint-Mars slept in a bed put up for him beside the bed of the man with the mask.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198829%E2%80%9330-147)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Bastille_floor_plan_labelled.png/250px-Bastille_floor_plan_labelled.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_floor_plan_labelled.png)

Plan of the Bastille in the 18th century. A – La Chapelle Tower; B – Trésor Tower; C – Comté Tower; D – Bazinière Tower; E – Bertaudière Tower; F – Liberté Tower; G – Puits Tower; H – Coin Tower; I – Courtyard of the Well; J – Office wing; K – Large Courtyard

Saint-Mars took up his new post on 18 September. His new second-in-command, Etienne Du Junca,[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196119-148) a _lieutenant de roi_[[s]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-lieutderoi-150) who kept a register of all prisoners held at the fortress, noted that the new governor "brought with him in his [palanquin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litter_(vehicle)#In_Europe "Litter (vehicle)") an old prisoner he had at Pignerol, whom he keeps always masked and whose name is not spoken".[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196112-151)

On his arrival, Dauger was placed temporarily in the first chamber on the first floor of the Bazinière Tower, located immediately to the left of the drawbridge, which usually served as a provisional accommodation for a few hours or a few days.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200423-152) At nine o'clock that evening, Du Junca and major Rosarges relocated him to a solitary cell in the pre-furnished third chamber on the third floor of the Bertaudière tower.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200423-152)[[t]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-bastcell-154) Rosarges, who had been part of Saint-Mars's staff since Pignerol,[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988110-155) was to continue taking care of the prisoner, and to feed him.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196113%E2%80%9314-156)

Du Junca's register confirms that the masked prisoner was kept in the third chamber of the Bertaudière Tower until 21 November 1699 and, despite extensive research into the Bastille archives, it is not known where he was relocated after that date. Modern historians believe that, given the poor soundproofing of the Bastille's cells, Saint-Mars must have decided to keep Dauger close to him in his residence adjacent to the fortress, in a small room that had already served as a prison in 1693, during the tenure of his predecessor, [François de Montlezun, Lord of Besmaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_the_Bastille#Fran%C3%A7ois_de_Montlezun "Governor of the Bastille").[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200425%E2%80%9326-157) According to evidence recorded by contemporaneous eye-witnesses, the masked prisoner used to go back and forth through the courtyard on his way to and from mass in the chapel located on the ground floor of the Liberty Tower, but other than that, nothing is known about his life in the Bastille.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200426-158)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988107-159)

A month or two before his death, he told the Bastille's doctor Fresquière:[[u]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-fresquier-162) "I believe I am sixty years old" ("Je crois avoir soixante ans").[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004166-121)[[v]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-marsolan-164) When he died, Du Junca logged the following entry in his register:

> On this day, Monday 19 November 1703, the unknown prisoner in the mask of black velvet who was brought here by the governor, M. de Saint-Mars, when he came from the island of Sainte-Marguerite, and who had been in his charge for a long time, felt a little unwell after attending mass and died today at 10 o'clock in the evening, without suffering a major disease. Surprised by death he did not receive the sacraments, but M. Giraut, the chaplain, had heard his confession the day before and exhorted him a little before he died."[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198832-165)

He was buried the next day under the name of "Marchioly" in the cemetery of the parish church of Saint-Paul in the presence of Rosarges and Abraham Reilhe, surgeon-major of the Bastille, who signed the death register, and the sum of 40 _livres_ was paid for his burial.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198833-4)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200426,_306-166)
