### Contemporaneous rumours

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Contemporaneous rumours")]

A week after Dauger's arrival at Pignerol, Saint-Mars wrote to Louvois (31 August 1669) reporting that the prisoner was rumoured to be a "[Marshall of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_of_France#Louis_XIV,_1643%E2%80%931715 "Marshall of France") or President of _[Parlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fronde\_(Parlement) "The Fronde (Parlement)")_".[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoux-Fazillac2018105-167)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961185-11)[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988257-168)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004181-169) Eight months later, Saint-Mars informed Louvois (12 April 1670) that he initiated some of these rumours himself, when asked about the prisoner: "I tell them tall tales to make fun of them."[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoux-Fazillac2018105-167)[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961186-170)[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988153-171)[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004182-172)

When Dauger was relocated to his third prison cell at the Île Sainte-Marguerite Fort in January 1687, Saint-Mars wrote to Louvois about the latest rumours (3 May 1687): "Everyone tries to guess who my prisoner might be."[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoux-Fazillac2018116-173)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaloy201816-174)[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961117%E2%80%93118-175)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200466-117)[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988265-176) On 4 September 1687, the _Nouvelles Écclésiastiques_ published a letter by Nicolas Fouquet's brother Louis, quoting a statement made by Saint-Mars: "All the people that one believes dead are not", a hint that the prisoner might be the [Duke of Beaufort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_de_Vend%C3%B4me,_duc_de_Beaufort "François de Vendôme, duc de Beaufort").[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAz%C3%A9ma1963150-177)[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrugnon19894-178)[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988264%E2%80%93266-179)[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004103%E2%80%93104-180) Four months later, Saint-Mars reiterated this rumour in writing to Louvois (8 January 1688), adding: "others say that he is a son of the late [Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell")".[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961120-181)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198859%E2%80%9367,_125,_132,_147-182)[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils200433,_191%E2%80%93192,_202,_215,_218,_220-183)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFr%C3%A9ron1768189-184)

#### Royal denial

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Royal denial")]

[Giacomo Casanova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Casanova "Giacomo Casanova"), in his autobiographical work _[Histoire de ma vie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histoire\_de\_ma\_vie "Histoire de ma vie")_, states that his French teacher and rival of Voltaire as a playwright, [Prosper Jolyot de Crébillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosper_Jolyot_de_Cr%C3%A9billon "Prosper Jolyot de Crébillon"), who had known Louis XIV and who was Royal Censor under [Louis XV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XV "Louis XV"), received from the Sun King the confidence that no Man in the Iron Mask had ever existed and that it was a legend. "According to Crébillon, the man in the iron mask was a fable; he said that Louis XIV had assured him of this with his own mouth."[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasanova2015Chapter_XXIV-185)

### English milord

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: English milord")]

On 10 October 1711, King Louis XIV's sister-in-law, [Elizabeth Charlotte, Princess Palatine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Charlotte,_Princess_Palatine "Elizabeth Charlotte, Princess Palatine"), sent a letter to her aunt, [Sophia, Electress of Hanover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophia_of_Hanover "Sophia of Hanover"), stating that the prisoner had "two [musketeers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musketeers "Musketeers") at his side to kill him if he removed his mask". She described him as very devout, and stated that he was well treated and received everything he desired.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196131-186) In another letter sent less than two weeks later, on 22 October, she added having just learnt that he was "an English milord connected with the affair of the [Duke of Berwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_FitzJames,_1st_Duke_of_Berwick "James FitzJames, 1st Duke of Berwick") against [King William III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_III_of_England "William III of England")."[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196131-186) The Princess was clearly reporting rumours she had heard at court.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196131%E2%80%9333,_236-187)[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBodemann1891288%E2%80%93293-188)

### King's relative

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: King's relative")]

Some of the most enduring theories about the prisoner's identity, outlined in the sections below, assume that he was a relative of Louis XIV, because of the importance attached to secrecy during his incarceration which, in turn, fed the legend that he must have been one of the most important persons in the realm.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196142-189) These theories emerged during the 1700s, long before historians were able to consult the archives revealing that the prisoner was "only a valet",[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961181%E2%80%93182-7) imprisoned for "what he was employed to do", and for "what he knew".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961190-68) These early theories arose solely from their author's imagination, and boosted the romantic appeal of a sensational elucidation of the enigma.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196140%E2%80%9352-190) Historians such as Mongrédien (1952) and Noone (1988), however, pointed out that the solution whereby Louis XIV is supposed to have had an illegitimate brother—whether older, twin, or younger—does not provide a credible explanation, for example, on how it would have been possible for Queen [Anne of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_of_Austria "Anne of Austria") to conceal a pregnancy throughout its full course and bear, then deliver, a child in secret.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196151-191)[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198845-192) Mongrédien concluded that "historians cannot give it the slightest credence."[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196152-193)

#### King's illegitimate son

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: King's illegitimate son")]

In 1745, an anonymous writer published a book in Amsterdam, _Mémoires pour servir à l'Histoire de la Perse_, romanticising life at the French Court in the form of Persian history. Members of the royal family and locations were given fictitious Persian names,[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196133-194) and their key was published in the book's third edition (1759).[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198851-195) In this tale, Louis XIV's illegitimate son, [Louis, Count of Vermandois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis,_Count_of_Vermandois "Louis, Count of Vermandois"), is alleged to have struck his half-brother, [Louis, Grand Dauphin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis,_Grand_Dauphin "Louis, Grand Dauphin"), causing the King to banish him to life imprisonment, first at the Île Sainte-Marguerite and later at the Bastille. He was made to wear a mask whenever he was to be seen or attended to, when sick or in other circumstances.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnonymous1745-196)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196133%E2%80%9337-197)[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198851%E2%80%9354-198) The theory of Vermandois as the prisoner in the mask was later mentioned by [Henri Griffet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Griffet "Henri Griffet"), in 1769, as having circulated during the reign of Louis XIV, therefore long before 1745.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGriffet1769323-199)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien1961236-200)

In reality, there are no historical records of gossip confirming that Vermandois ever struck the Grand Dauphin.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196137%E2%80%9338-201)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198854-202) In the memoirs of Louis XIV's first cousin, the [Duchess of Montpensier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Marie_Louise_d'Orl%C3%A9ans,_Duchess_of_Montpensier "Anne Marie Louise d'Orléans, Duchess of Montpensier"), there is mention of Vermandois having displeased the King for taking part in orgies in 1682, and being temporarily banished from court as a result. After promising to mend his way, he was sent—soon after his 16th birthday—to join the army in [Courtrai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtrai "Courtrai") during the [War of the Reunions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Reunions "War of the Reunions") (1683–84), in early November 1683. He distinguished himself in the battle line, but died of a fever during the night of 17 November. Louis XIV was reported to be deeply affected by his son's death, and Vermandois' sister, [Marie Anne de Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Anne_de_Bourbon "Marie Anne de Bourbon"), was inconsolable while their mother, [Louise de La Vallière](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_de_La_Valli%C3%A8re "Louise de La Vallière"), sought solace in endless prayer at her [Carmelites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmelites "Carmelites")[convent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Couvent_des_Carm%C3%A9lites_du_faubourg_Saint-Jacques "Couvent des Carmélites du faubourg Saint-Jacques") in Paris.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196138%E2%80%9339-203)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198851-195)

#### King's elder brother

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: King's elder brother")]

During his two sojourns in the Bastille in 1717–18 and 1726,[[w]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-voltaire-208) Voltaire became aware of the traditions and legends circulating among the staff at the fortress.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196140%E2%80%9341-209) On 30 October 1738, he wrote to the [Abbé Dubos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Baptiste_Dubos "Jean-Baptiste Dubos"): "I am somewhat knowledgeable about the adventure of the Man in the Iron Mask, who died at the Bastille; I spoke to people who had served him."[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196141,_237-210) In the second edition of his _Questions sur l'Encyclopédie_ (1771), Voltaire claimed that the prisoner was an illegitimate first son of Anne of Austria and an unknown father, and therefore an older half-brother of Louis XIV.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196147%E2%80%9348-211) This assertion was partly based on the historical fact that the birth of Louis XIV on 5 September 1638 had come as a surprise: since [Louis XIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIII "Louis XIII") and Anne of Austria had been childless for 23 years, it was believed they were unable to conceive, despite evidence to the contrary of the queen's well-known miscarriages.[[x]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-annemisc-218)[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196147%E2%80%9349-219) In fact, the royal couple had been living for years in mutual distrust and had become estranged since the mid-1620s. Furthermore, in August 1637, the Queen had been found guilty of treasonable correspondence with Spain and had been placed under house arrest at the [Louvre Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre_Palace "Louvre Palace").[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198842-220) However, contemporaneous accounts nonetheless indicate that the royal couple shared a bed and conceived the future Louis XIV, either in early December 1637[[y]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-dec1637-223) or, as historians deem more likely, sometime during the previous month.[[z]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-nov1637-225)[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKleinman1993194-224)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMansel202217-226) The Queen's pregnancy was made public on 30 January 1638.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMansel202217-226)

Based on the assumption that the royal couple were unable to conceive, Voltaire theorised that an earlier, secret birth of an illegitimate child persuaded the Queen that she was not infertile, in turn prompting [Cardinal Richelieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Richelieu "Cardinal Richelieu") to arrange an outing during which the royal couple had to share a bed, which led to the birth of Louis XIV.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVoltaire1770%E2%80%931771-227)[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarra1789315%E2%80%93321-228)[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTECraufurd1790254%E2%80%93356-229)[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196140%E2%80%9349-230)

The theme of an imagined elder brother of Louis XIV resurfaced in 1790, when French historian Pierre-Hubert Charpentier asserted that the prisoner was an illegitimate son of Anne of Austria and [George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Villiers,_1st_Duke_of_Buckingham "George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham"), supposedly born in 1626, two years before the latter's death.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTECharpentierManuel1790140%E2%80%93162-231)[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196150-232)[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone198843%E2%80%9345-233) Louis XIV was presumed to have had this elder brother imprisoned upon the Queen's death in 1666. According to Charpentier, this theory had originated with a certain Mademoiselle de Saint-Quentin, a mistress of the [Marquess of Barbezieux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Fran%C3%A7ois_Marie_Le_Tellier "Louis François Marie Le Tellier"), son of Louvois and his successor as War Minister to Louis XIV in 1691.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196150-232) A few days before his sudden death on 5 January 1701, Barbezieux had told her the secret of the prisoner's identity, which she disclosed publicly to several people in [Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres "Chartres") towards the end of her life in the mid-1700s. Charpentier also stated that Voltaire had heard this version in [Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva "Geneva"), but chose to omit Buckingham's name when he began to develop his own variant of this theory in the first edition of _[The Age of Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Age\_of\_Louis\_XIV "The Age of Louis XIV")_ (1751),[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTECharpentierManuel1790140%E2%80%93162-231) finally revealed in full in _Questions sur l'Encyclopédie_ (1771).[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTECharpentierManuel1790140%E2%80%93162-231)

#### King's twin brother

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: King's twin brother")]

Many authors supported the theory of the prisoner being a twin brother of Louis XIV: [Michel de Cubières](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_de_Cubi%C3%A8res "Michel de Cubières") (1789), [Jean-Louis Soulavie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Louis_Giraud_Soulavie "Jean-Louis Giraud Soulavie") (1791), [Las Cases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel,_comte_de_Las_Cases "Emmanuel, comte de Las Cases") (1816), [Victor Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Hugo "Victor Hugo") (1839), Alexandre Dumas (1840), Paul Lecointe (1847), and others.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196151-191)

In a 1965 essay, _Le Masque de fer_ (revised in 1973 under the title _[Le secret du Masque de Fer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_secret\_du\_Masque\_de\_Fer "Le secret du Masque de Fer")_), French novelist and playwright [Marcel Pagnol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Pagnol "Marcel Pagnol"), proposing his hypothesis in particular on the circumstances of Louis XIV's birth, claimed that the Man in the Iron Mask was indeed a twin brother, but born second, who would have been hidden in order to avoid any dispute over the throne holder.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPagnol197319%E2%80%9322-234) At the time, there was a controversy over which one of twins was the elder: the one born first, or the one born second, who was then thought to have been conceived first.[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPagnol1973289%E2%80%93290,_334-235)

Historians who reject this hypothesis (including [Jean-Christian Petitfils](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Christian%20Petitfils "fr:Jean-Christian Petitfils")) highlight the conditions of childbirth for the Queen: it usually took place in the presence of multiple witnesses—the main court's figures. According to Pagnol, immediately after the birth of the future Louis XIV at 11 a.m. on 5 September 1638, Louis XIII took his whole court (about 40 people) to the [_Château de Saint-Germain_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Saint-Germain-en-Laye "Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye")'s chapel to celebrate a _[Te Deum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te\_Deum "Te Deum")_ in great pomp,[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPagnol197319%E2%80%9322-234) contrary to the common practice of celebrating it several days before childbirth.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDumont1739-236) Pagnol contends that the court's removal to this _Te Deum_ had been rushed to enable the Queen to deliver the second twin in secret and attended only by the midwife.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPagnol197319%E2%80%9322-234)

Pagnol's solution—combining earlier theories by [Soulavie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Louis_Giraud_Soulavie "Jean-Louis Giraud Soulavie") (1790),[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTESoulavie1790-237)[Andrew Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Lang "Andrew Lang") (1903),[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTELang2002-238)[Arthur Barnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Barnes_(monsignor) "Arthur Barnes (monsignor)") (1908),[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes1908-239) and Edith Carey (1924)[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey1924-240)—speculates that this twin was born a few hours after Louis XIV and grew up on the Island of [Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey "Jersey") under the name [James de la Cloche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_de_la_Cloche "James de la Cloche"), believing himself to be an illegitimate son of [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"). During a hypothetical, secret meeting in January 1669, Charles is assumed to have recognised the twin for his resemblance to the French king and revealed to him his true identity.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPagnol1973330%E2%80%93334-241) Shortly thereafter, the twin would supposedly have adopted the new identity of "Martin" as a valet to [Roux de Marcilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roux_de_Marcilly "Roux de Marcilly"), with whom he conspired against Louis XIV, which led to his arrest in Calais in July 1669.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPagnol1973137%E2%80%93165-242) Historically, however, the real valet Martin (distinct from Pagnol's reinterpreted "Martin") could not have become "Eustache Dauger" because he had fled to London when the Roux conspiracy failed; this is well known because his extradition from England to France had at first been requested by Foreign Minister [Hugues de Lionne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugues_de_Lionne "Hugues de Lionne") on 12 June 1669, but subsequently cancelled by him on 13 July.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoone1988187-243) Pagnol explained this historical fact away by claiming, without any evidence, that "Martin" must have been secretly abducted in London in early July and transported to France on 7 or 8 July, and that the extradition order had therefore been cancelled because it was no longer necessary, its objective having already been achieved.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPagnol1973155%E2%80%93156-244)

#### King's younger brother

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: King's younger brother")]

In 1791, Jean Baptiste De Saint-Mihiel proposed that the prisoner was an illegitimate younger brother of Louis XIV, fathered by [Cardinal Mazarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Mazarin "Cardinal Mazarin").[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196151-191) This theory was based on the fact, mentioned by Voltaire in _Questions sur l'Encyclopédie_ (1771), that the prisoner had told his doctor that he "believed himself to be about 60 years old", a few days before his death in 1703. De Saint-Mihiel extrapolated that the prisoner was therefore born around 1643, and could therefore only be a younger brother to the King, born in 1638.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetitfils2004224%E2%80%93225-245) It is a historical fact that, four days after Louis XIII's death on 14 May 1643, Anne of Austria was declared Regent and appointed Mazarin as her chief minister and head of government that evening.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDethan195950%E2%80%9351-246) Mazarin was soon believed to be her lover, and even her secret [morganatic husband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morganatic_marriage "Morganatic marriage").[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTETreasure1984216%E2%80%93217-247) The theory of the prisoner being an imagined, younger son of the Queen and Mazarin was rekindled in 1868 by Charles-Henri, baron de Gleichen.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleichenGrimblot186846%E2%80%9350-248)[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMongr%C3%A9dien196151-191)

#### King's father

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Man_in_the_Iron_Mask&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: King's father")]

In 1955, Hugh Ross Williamson argued that the Man in the Iron Mask was the natural father of Louis XIV. According to this theory, the "miraculous" birth of Louis XIV in 1638 would have come after Louis XIII had been estranged from his wife Anne of Austria for 14 years.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002245-249)

The theory then suggests that Cardinal Richelieu had arranged for a substitute, probably an illegitimate grandson of [Henry IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_France "Henry IV of France"),[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002247-250) to become intimate with the Queen and father an heir in the King's stead. At the time, the [heir presumptive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heir_presumptive "Heir presumptive") was Louis XIII's brother [Gaston, Duke of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaston,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Gaston, Duke of Orléans"), who was Richelieu's enemy. If Gaston became king, Richelieu would quite likely have lost both his job as minister and his life, and so it was in his best interests to thwart Gaston's ambitions.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002246-251)

Supposedly, the substitute father then left for the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_France "New France") but returned to France in the 1660s with the aim of extorting money for keeping his secret and was promptly imprisoned. This theory would explain the secrecy surrounding the prisoner, whose true identity would have destroyed the legitimacy of Louis XIV's claim to the throne had it been revealed.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002247%E2%80%93248-252)

This theory had been suggested by British politician [Hugh Cecil, 1st Baron Quickswood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Cecil,_1st_Baron_Quickswood "Hugh Cecil, 1st Baron Quickswood"), who nonetheless added that the idea has no historical basis and is entirely hypothetical.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002245-249) Williamson held that: "to say it is a guess with no solid historical basis is merely to say that it is like every other theory on the matter, although it makes more sense than any of the other theories. There is no known evidence that is incompatible with it, even the age of the prisoner, which Cecil had considered a weak point;[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002249%E2%80%93251-253) and it explains every aspect of the mystery."[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson2002245-249) His time spent as a valet to another prisoner renders this idea doubtful, however.[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Iron_Mask#cite_note-valet-67)

#### Philippe d'Orléans's younger brother

Fortress in Paris (1370 – 1789/90)

This article is about the fortress in Paris. For the fall of the Bastille in the French Revolution, see [Storming of the Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storming_of_the_Bastille "Storming of the Bastille"). The **Bastille** ([/b æ ˈ s t iː l/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"), French:[[bastij]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/5/5b/LL-Q150_%28fra%29-Ltrlg-Bastille.wav/LL-Q150_%28fra%29-Ltrlg-Bastille.wav.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LL-Q150_(fra)-Ltrlg-Bastille.wav "File:LL-Q150 (fra)-Ltrlg-Bastille.wav")) was a medieval fortress in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), known as the **Bastille Saint-Antoine**. It played an important role in the internal conflicts of France and for most of its history was used as a state [prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prison "Prison") by the [kings of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_French_monarchs "List of French monarchs"). It was [stormed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storming_of_the_Bastille "Storming of the Bastille") by a crowd on 14 July 1789, in the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution"), becoming an important symbol for the French [Republican movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Left_in_France#19th_century "History of the Left in France"). It was later demolished and replaced by the [Place de la Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_de_la_Bastille "Place de la Bastille") public square in Paris.

The castle was built to defend the eastern approach to the city from potential English attacks during the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War "Hundred Years' War"). Construction was underway by 1357, but the main construction occurred from 1370 onwards, creating a strong fortress with eight towers that protected the strategic gateway of the [Porte Saint-Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porte_Saint-Antoine "Porte Saint-Antoine") heading out to the east. The innovative design proved influential in both France and England and was widely copied. The Bastille figured prominently in France's domestic conflicts, including the fighting between the rival factions of the [Burgundians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Burgundy "Duchy of Burgundy") and the [Armagnacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armagnac_(party) "Armagnac (party)") in the 15th century, and the [Wars of Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion "French Wars of Religion") in the 16th. The fortress was declared a state prison in 1417; this role was expanded further, first under the [English occupiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England "Henry V of England") of the 1420s and 1430s, and then under [Louis XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XI "Louis XI") in the 1460s. The defences of the Bastille were fortified in response to the [Imperial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") threat during the 1550s, with a [bastion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion") constructed to the east of the fortress. The Bastille played a key role in the rebellion of the [Fronde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fronde "Fronde") and the [Battle of the Faubourg St Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Faubourg_St_Antoine "Battle of the Faubourg St Antoine"), which was fought beneath its walls in 1652.

[Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV "Louis XIV") used the Bastille as a prison for upper-class members of French society who had opposed or angered him including, after the [revocation of the Edict of Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revocation_of_the_Edict_of_Nantes "Revocation of the Edict of Nantes"), French [Protestants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant "Protestant"). From 1659 onwards, the Bastille functioned primarily as a state penitentiary; by 1789, 5,279 prisoners had passed through its gates. Under [Louis XV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XV "Louis XV") and [XVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XVI "Louis XVI"), the Bastille was used to detain prisoners from more varied backgrounds, and to support the operations of the Parisian police, especially in enforcing government censorship of the printed media. Although inmates were kept in relatively good conditions, criticism of the Bastille grew during the 18th century, fuelled by autobiographies written by former prisoners. Reforms were implemented and prisoner numbers were considerably reduced.

In 1789, the royal government's financial crisis and the formation of the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(French_Revolution) "National Assembly (French Revolution)") gave rise to a swelling of republican sentiments among city-dwellers. On 14 July, the Bastille was [stormed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storming_of_the_Bastille "Storming of the Bastille") by a revolutionary crowd, primarily residents of the [Faubourg Saint-Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faubourg_Saint-Antoine "Faubourg Saint-Antoine") who sought to commandeer the valuable gunpowder held within the fortress. Seven remaining prisoners were found and released and the Bastille's governor, [Bernard-René de Launay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard-Ren%C3%A9_de_Launay "Bernard-René de Launay"), was killed by the crowd. The Bastille was demolished by order of the [Committee of the Hôtel de Ville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_de_Ville,_Paris "Hôtel de Ville, Paris"). Souvenirs of the fortress were transported around France and displayed as icons of the overthrow of [despotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotism "Despotism"). Over the next century, the site and historical legacy of the Bastille featured prominently in French [revolutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_Revolution "July Revolution"), political protests and popular fiction, and it remained an important symbol for the French [Republican movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Left_in_France#19th_century "History of the Left in France").

Almost nothing is left of the Bastille, except some remains of its stone foundation that were relocated to the side of Boulevard Henri IV. Historians were critical of the Bastille in the early 19th century, and believe the fortress to have been a relatively well-administered example of French policing and political control during the 18th century.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### 14th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 14th century")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Bastille_reconstruction_1420.jpg/330px-Bastille_reconstruction_1420.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_reconstruction_1420.jpg)

Historical reconstruction showing the moat below the walls of Paris (left), the Bastille and the [Porte Saint-Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porte_Saint-Antoine "Porte Saint-Antoine") (right) in 1420

The Bastille was built to defend Paris during the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War "Hundred Years' War") between France and England.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-LandsdaleP216-1) Prior to the Bastille, the main royal castle in Paris was the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre "Louvre"), in the west of the capital, but the city had expanded by the middle of the 14th century and the eastern side was now vulnerable to English attacks.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-LandsdaleP216-1) The situation worsened after the [imprisonment of John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom_of_John_II_of_France "Ransom of John II of France") in England following the French defeat at the [Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers"), and in his absence the [Provost of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provost_of_Paris "Provost of Paris"), [Étienne Marcel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tienne_Marcel "Étienne Marcel"), took steps to improve the capital's defences.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-2) In 1357, Marcel expanded the city walls and protected the [Porte Saint-Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porte_Saint-Antoine "Porte Saint-Antoine") with two high stone towers and a 78-foot-wide (24 m) ditch.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-3)[[A]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-5) A fortified gateway of this sort was called a _bastille_, and was one of two created in Paris, the other being built outside the [Porte Saint-Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porte_Saint-Denis "Porte Saint-Denis").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-6) Marcel was subsequently removed from his post and executed in 1358.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-ViolletLandsdaleP218-7)

In 1369, Charles V became concerned about the vulnerability of the eastern side of Paris to potential attacks by English forces and mercenaries.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-8) Charles instructed [Hugues Aubriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugues_Aubriot "Hugues Aubriot"), the new provost, to build a much larger fortification on the same site as Marcel's _bastille_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-ViolletLandsdaleP218-7) Work began in 1370 with another pair of towers being built behind the first _bastille_, followed by two towers to the north, and finally two towers to the south.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CouereteBournonP3-9) The fortress was probably not finished by the time Charles died in 1380, and was completed by his son, [Charles VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VI_of_France "Charles VI of France").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CouereteBournonP3-9) The resulting structure became known simply as the Bastille, with the eight irregularly built towers and linking curtain walls forming a structure 223 feet (68 m) wide and 121 feet (37 m) deep, the walls and towers 78 feet (24 m) high and 10 feet (3.0 m) thick at their bases.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-10) Built to the same height, the roofs of the towers and the tops of the walls formed a broad, [crenellated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crenellated "Crenellated") walkway all the way around the fortress.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Anderson,_p._208-11) Each of the six newer towers had underground _cachots_, or [dungeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dungeon "Dungeon"), at its base, and curved _calotte_, literally "shell", rooms in their roofs.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-12)

Garrisoned by a captain, a knight, eight squires and ten crossbowmen, the Bastille was encircled with ditches fed by the River [Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine "Seine"), and faced with stone.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-13) The fortress had four sets of drawbridges, which allowed the Rue Saint-Antoine to pass eastwards through the Bastille's gates while giving easy access to the city walls on the north and south sides.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-14) The Bastille overlooked the Saint-Antoine gate, which by 1380 was a strong, square building with turrets and protected by two drawbridges of its own.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-15) Charles V chose to live close to the Bastille for his own safety and created a royal complex to the south of the fortress called the [Hôtel Saint-Pol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_Saint-Pol "Hôtel Saint-Pol"), stretching from the Porte Saint-Paul up to the Rue Saint-Antoine.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-16)[[B]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-17)

Historian [Sidney Toy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Toy "Sidney Toy") has described the Bastille as "one of the most powerful fortifications" of the period, and the most important fortification in late medieval Paris.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-18) The Bastille's design was highly innovative: it rejected both the 13th-century tradition of more weakly fortified [quadrangular castles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrangular_castle "Quadrangular castle"), and the contemporary fashion set at [Vincennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Vincennes "Château de Vincennes"), where tall towers were positioned around a lower wall, overlooked by an even taller keep in the centre.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Anderson,_p._208-11) In particular, building the towers and the walls of the Bastille at the same height allowed the rapid movement of forces around the castle, as well as giving more space to move and position cannons on the wider walkways.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-19) The Bastille design was copied at [Pierrefonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Pierrefonds "Château de Pierrefonds") and [Tarascon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarascon_castle "Tarascon castle") in France, while its architectural influence extended as far as [Nunney Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nunney_Castle "Nunney Castle") in south-west England.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-20)

### 15th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 15th century")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Bastille_in_Medieval_Paris_Map..png/250px-Bastille_in_Medieval_Paris_Map..png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_in_Medieval_Paris_Map..png)

Parisian defences in 14th century: A – [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre_Palace "Louvre Palace"); B – Palais de Roi; C – Hôtel des Tournelles; D – [Porte Saint-Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porte_Saint-Antoine "Porte Saint-Antoine"); E – Hôtel St Paul; F – the Bastille

During the 15th century, the French kings continued to engage in conflict with the English, [Burgundians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Burgundy "Duchy of Burgundy") and [Armagnacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armagnac_(party) "Armagnac (party)").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-21) The Bastille was strategically vital during the period, both because of its role as a royal fortress and safe-haven inside the capital, and because it controlled a critical route in and out of Paris.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-22) In 1418, for example, the future [Charles VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VII_of_France "Charles VII of France") took refuge in the Bastille during the Burgundian-led "[Massacre of the Armagnacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_coup_d'%C3%A9tat_and_massacres_of_1418 "Paris coup d'état and massacres of 1418")" in Paris, before successfully fleeing the city through the Porte Saint-Antoine.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-23) The Bastille was occasionally used to hold prisoners, including its creator, [Hugues Aubriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugues_Aubriot "Hugues Aubriot"), who was the first person to be imprisoned there. In 1417, in addition to being a royal fortress, it formally became a state prison.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP4-24)[[C]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-26)

Despite the improved Parisian defences, [Henry V of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England "Henry V of England") captured Paris in 1420 and the Bastille was garrisoned by the English for the next sixteen years.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP4-24) Henry V appointed [Thomas Beaufort, Duke of Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Beaufort,_Duke_of_Exeter "Thomas Beaufort, Duke of Exeter"), as the new captain of the Bastille.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP4-24) The English made more use of the Bastille as a prison; in 1430 there was a minor rebellion when some prisoners overpowered a sleeping guard and attempted to seize control of the fortress; this incident includes the first reference to a dedicated gaoler at the Bastille.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-27)

Paris was finally recaptured by Charles VII of France in 1436. When the French king re-entered the city, his enemies in Paris fortified themselves in the Bastille; after a siege, they eventually ran out of food, surrendered and were allowed to leave the city after the payment of a ransom.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-28) The castle remained a key Parisian fortress, but was successfully seized by the Burgundians in 1464, when they convinced royal troops to surrender: once taken, this allowed their faction to make a surprise attack into Paris, almost resulting in the capture of the king.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-29)

The Bastille was being used to hold prisoners once again by the reign of [Louis XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XI "Louis XI"), who began to use it extensively as a state penitentiary.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-30) An early escapee from the Bastille during this period was [Antoine de Chabannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_de_Chabannes "Antoine de Chabannes"), Count of Dammartin and a member of the [League of the Public Weal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_the_Public_Weal "League of the Public Weal"), who was imprisoned by Louis and escaped by boat in 1465.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-31) The captains of the Bastille during this period were primarily officers and royal functionaries; Philippe de [Melun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melun "Melun") was the first captain to receive a salary in 1462, being awarded 1,200 [livres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_livre "French livre") a year.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-32)[[D]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-34) Despite being a state prison, the Bastille retained the other traditional functions of a royal castle, and was used to accommodate visiting dignitaries, hosting some lavish entertainments given by Louis XI and [Francis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_I_of_France "Francis I of France").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-35)

### 16th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 16th century")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Bastille_district_1575.jpg/500px-Bastille_district_1575.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_district_1575.jpg)

A depiction of the Bastille and neighbouring Paris in 1575, showing the new [bastions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion"), the new Porte Saint-Antoine, the [Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_of_Paris?action=edit&redlink=1 "Arsenal of Paris (page does not exist)") complex and the open countryside beyond the city defences

During the 16th century the area around the Bastille developed further. Early modern Paris continued to grow, and by the end of the century it had around 250,000 inhabitants and was one of the most populous cities in Europe, though still largely contained within its old city walls – open countryside remained beyond the Bastille.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-36) The [Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_of_Paris?action=edit&redlink=1 "Arsenal of Paris (page does not exist)"), a large military-industrial complex tasked with the production of cannons and other weapons for the royal armies, was established to the south of the Bastille by Francis I, and substantially expanded under [Charles IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_IX_of_France "Charles IX of France").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-37) An arms depot was later built above the Porte Saint-Antoine, all making the Bastille part of a major military centre.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-38)

During the 1550s, [Henry II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_II_of_France "Henry II of France") became concerned about the possibility of an attack on Paris by England or the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), and strengthened the defences of the Bastille in response.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-39) The southern gateway into the Bastille became the principal entrance to the castle in 1553, the other three gateways being closed.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP4-24) A [bastion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion"), a large earthwork projecting eastwards from the Bastille, was built to provide additional [protective fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suppressive_fire "Suppressive fire") for the Bastille and the Arsenal; the bastion was reached from the fortress across a stone [abutment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abutment "Abutment") using a connecting drawbridge that was installed in the Bastille's Comté tower.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-40) In 1573 the Porte Saint-Antoine was also altered – the drawbridges were replaced with a fixed bridge, and the medieval gatehouse was replaced with a [triumphal arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triumphal_arch "Triumphal arch").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-41)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Callot_view_of_the_Bastille.jpg/250px-Callot_view_of_the_Bastille.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Callot_view_of_the_Bastille.jpg)

The Bastille in 1647, illustrating the bastion, the stone [abutment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abutment "Abutment") linking to the fortress and the new southern entrance built during the 1550s

The Bastille was involved in the numerous [wars of religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion "French Wars of Religion") fought between Protestant and Catholic factions with support from foreign allies during the second half of the 16th century. Religious and political tensions in Paris initially exploded in the [Day of the Barricades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Barricades "Day of the Barricades") on 12 May 1588, when hard-line Catholics rose up in revolt against the relatively moderate [Henry III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_III_of_France "Henry III of France"). After a day's fighting had occurred across the capital, Henry III fled and the Bastille surrendered to [Henry I, Duke of Guise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_I,_Duke_of_Guise "Henry I, Duke of Guise"), the leader of the [Catholic League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_League_(French) "Catholic League (French)"), who appointed Bussy-Leclerc as his new captain.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-42) Henry III responded by having the Duke and his brother murdered later that year, whereupon Bussy-Leclerc used the Bastille as a base to mount a raid on the [Parlement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlement_of_Paris "Parlement of Paris"), arresting the president and other magistrates, whom he suspected of having royalist sympathies, and detaining them in the Bastille.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-43) They were not released until the intervention of [Charles, Duke of Mayenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Mayenne "Charles, Duke of Mayenne"), and the payment of substantial ransoms.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-44) Bussy-Leclerc remained in control of the Bastille until December 1592, when, following further political instability, he was forced to surrender the castle to Charles and flee the city.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-45)

It took [Henry IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_France "Henry IV of France") several years to retake Paris. By the time he succeeded in 1594, the area around the Bastille formed the main stronghold for the Catholic League and their foreign allies, including Spanish and Flemish troops.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-46) The Bastille itself was controlled by a League captain called du Bourg.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-47) Henry entered Paris early on the morning of 23 March, through the Porte-Neuve rather than the Saint-Antoine and seized the capital, including the Arsenal complex that neighboured the Bastille.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-48) The Bastille was now an isolated League stronghold, with the remaining members of the League and their allies clustering around it for safety.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-49) After several days of tension, an agreement was finally reached for this rump element to leave safely, and on 27 March du Bourg surrendered the Bastille and left the city himself.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-50)

### Early 17th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Early 17th century")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Episode_of_the_Fronde_at_the_Faubourg_Saint-Antoine_by_the_Walls_of_the_Bastille.png/250px-Episode_of_the_Fronde_at_the_Faubourg_Saint-Antoine_by_the_Walls_of_the_Bastille.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Episode_of_the_Fronde_at_the_Faubourg_Saint-Antoine_by_the_Walls_of_the_Bastille.png)

A contemporary depiction of the [battle of the Faubourg St Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Faubourg_St_Antoine "Battle of the Faubourg St Antoine") beneath the walls of the Bastille in 1652

The Bastille continued to be used as a prison and a royal fortress under both Henry IV and his son, [Louis XIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIII "Louis XIII"). When Henry clamped down on a Spanish-backed plot among the senior [French nobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_nobility "French nobility") in 1602, for example, he detained the ringleader [Charles de Gontaut, duc de Biron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gontaut,_duc_de_Biron "Charles de Gontaut, duc de Biron"), in the Bastille, and had him executed in the courtyard.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-51) Louis XIII's chief minister, [Cardinal Richelieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Richelieu "Cardinal Richelieu"), is credited with beginning the modern transformation of the Bastille into a more formal organ of the French state, further increasing its structured use as a state prison.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-52) Richelieu broke with Henry IV's tradition of the Bastille's captain being a member of the French aristocracy, typically a [Marshal of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshal_of_France "Marshal of France") such as [François de Bassompierre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_de_Bassompierre "François de Bassompierre"), [Charles d'Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_d'Albert,_duc_de_Luynes "Charles d'Albert, duc de Luynes") or [Nicolas de L'Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_de_L'Hospital "Nicolas de L'Hospital"), and instead appointed [Père Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Leclerc_du_Tremblay "François Leclerc du Tremblay")'s brother to run the facility.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-53)[[E]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-55) The first surviving documentary records of prisoners at the Bastille also date from this period.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-56)

In 1648, the [Fronde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fronde "Fronde") insurrection broke out in Paris, prompted by high taxes, increased food prices and disease.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Munck,_p._212-57) The _Parlement of Paris_, the Regency government of [Anne of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_of_Austria "Anne of Austria") and rebellious noble factions fought for several years to take control of the city and wider power. On 26 August, during the period known as the First Fronde, Anne ordered the arrest of some of the leaders of the Parlement of Paris; violence flared as a result, and the 27 August became known as another [Day of the Barricades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Barricades "Day of the Barricades").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-58) The governor of the Bastille loaded and readied his guns to fire on the [Hôtel de Ville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_de_Ville,_Paris "Hôtel de Ville, Paris"), controlled by the parliament, although the decision was eventually taken not to shoot.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-59) Barricades were erected across the city and the royal government fled in September, leaving a garrison of 22 men behind in the Bastille.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-60) On 11 January 1649, the Fronde decided to take the Bastille, giving the task to Elbeuf, one of their leaders.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-61) Elbeuf's attack required only a token effort: five or six shots were fired at the Bastille, before it promptly surrendered on 13 January.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-62)[Pierre Broussel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Broussel "Pierre Broussel"), one of the Fronde leaders, appointed his son as the governor and the Fronde retained it even after the ceasefire that March.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-63)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Bastille_1649.jpg/500px-Bastille_1649.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_1649.jpg)

The Bastille and the eastern side of Paris in 1649

During the Second Fronde, between 1650 and 1653, [Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis,_Grand_Cond%C3%A9 "Louis, Grand Condé"), the Prince of Condé, controlled much of Paris alongside the Parlement, while Broussel, through his son, continued to control the Bastille. In July 1652, the [Battle of the Faubourg St Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Faubourg_St_Antoine "Battle of the Faubourg St Antoine") took place just outside the Bastille. Condé had sallied out of Paris to prevent the advance of the royalist forces under the command of [Turenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_la_Tour_d'Auvergne,_Vicomte_de_Turenne "Henri de la Tour d'Auvergne, Vicomte de Turenne").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-64) Condé's forces became trapped against the city walls and the Porte Saint-Antoine, which the Parlement refused to open; he was coming under increasingly heavy fire from the Royalist artillery and the situation looked bleak.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-65) In a famous incident, [La Grande Mademoiselle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Marie_Louise_d'Orl%C3%A9ans,_Duchess_of_Montpensier "Anne Marie Louise d'Orléans, Duchess of Montpensier"), the daughter of [Gaston, Duke of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaston,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Gaston, Duke of Orléans"), convinced her father to issue an order for the Parisian forces to act, before she then entered the Bastille and personally ensured that the commander turned the fortress's cannon on Turenne's army, causing significant casualties and enabling Condé's army's safe withdrawal.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-66) Later in 1652, Condé was finally forced to surrender Paris to the royalist forces in October, effectively bringing the Fronde to an end: the Bastille returned to royal control.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Munck,_p._212-57)

### Reign of Louis XIV and the Regency (1661–1723)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Reign of Louis XIV and the Regency (1661–1723)")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Bastille_1715.jpg/500px-Bastille_1715.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_1715.jpg)

The Bastille and Porte Saint-Antoine from the north-east, 1715–19

The area around the Bastille was transformed in the reign of Louis XIV. Paris' growing population reached 400,000 during the period, causing the city to spill out past the Bastille and the old city into the arable farmland beyond, forming more thinly populated _[faubourgs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faubourg "Faubourg")_, or suburbs.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-67) Influenced by the events of the Fronde, Louis XIV rebuilt the area around the Bastille, erecting a new archway at the Porte Saint-Antoine in 1660, and then ten years later pulling down the city walls and their supporting fortifications to replace them with an avenue of trees, later called Louis XIV's boulevard, which passed around the Bastille.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-68) The Bastille's bastion survived the redevelopment, becoming a garden for the use of the prisoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-69)

Louis XIV made extensive use of the Bastille as a prison, with 2,320 individuals being detained there during his reign, approximately 43 a year.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-BNF1-70) Louis used the Bastille to hold not just suspected rebels or plotters but also those who had simply irritated him in some way, such as differing with him on matters of religion.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-71) The typical offences that inmates were accused of were espionage, counterfeiting and embezzlement from the state; a number of financial officials were detained in this way under Louis, most famously including [Nicolas Fouquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Fouquet "Nicolas Fouquet"), his supporters [Henry de Guénegaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_de_Gu%C3%A9negaud "Henry de Guénegaud"), Jeannin and [Lorenzo de Tonti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenzo_de_Tonti "Lorenzo de Tonti").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-72) In 1685 Louis [revoked the Edict of Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Fontainebleau "Edict of Fontainebleau"), which had previously granted various rights to French Protestants; the subsequent royal crackdown was driven by the king's strongly anti-Protestant views.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-73) The Bastille was used to investigate and break up Protestant networks by imprisoning and questioning the more recalcitrant members of the community, in particular upper-class [Calvinists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinist "Calvinist"); some 254 Protestants were imprisoned in the Bastille during Louis's reign.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-74)

By Louis's reign, Bastille prisoners were detained using a _[lettre de cachet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lettre\_de\_cachet "Lettre de cachet")_, a letter under royal seal, issued by the king and countersigned by a minister, ordering a named person to be held.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-TroutP142-75) Louis, closely involved in this aspect of government, personally decided who should be imprisoned at the Bastille.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-BNF1-70) The arrest itself involved an element of ceremony: the individual would be tapped on the shoulder with a white baton and formally detained in the name of the king.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-TroutP143-76) Detention in the Bastille was typically ordered for an indefinite period and there was considerable secrecy over who had been detained and why: the legend of the "Man in the Iron Mask", a mysterious prisoner who finally died in 1703, symbolises this period of the Bastille.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-77) Although in practice many were held at the Bastille as a form of punishment, legally a prisoner in the Bastille was only being detained for preventative or investigative reasons: the prison was not officially supposed to be a punitive measure in its own right.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-TroutP141-78) The average length of imprisonment in the Bastille under Louis XIV was approximately three years.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-LusebrinkP51-79)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Bastille%2C_1734.jpg/250px-Bastille%2C_1734.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille,_1734.jpg)

The Bastille in 1734, showing the Louis XIV boulevard and the growing "[faubourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faubourg "Faubourg")" beyond the Porte Saint-Antoine

Under Louis, only between 20 and 50 prisoners were usually held at the Bastille at any one time, although as many as 111 were held for a short period in 1703.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-TroutP142-75) These prisoners were mainly from the upper classes, and those who could afford to pay for additional luxuries lived in good conditions, wearing their own clothes, living in rooms decorated with tapestries and carpets or taking exercise around the castle garden and along the walls.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-TroutP141-78) By the late 17th century, there was a rather disorganised library for the use of inmates in the Bastille, although its origins remain unclear.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-80)[[F]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-82)

Louis reformed the administrative structure of the Bastille, creating the post of governor, although this post was still often referred to as the captain-governor.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-83) During Louis's reign the policing of marginal groups in Paris was greatly increased: the wider criminal justice system was reformed, controls over printing and publishing extended, new criminal codes were issued and the post of the Parisian [lieutenant general of police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefecture_of_Police "Prefecture of Police") was created in 1667, all of which would enable the Bastille's later role in support of the Parisian police during the 18th century.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-84) By 1711, a 60-strong French military garrison had been established at the Bastille.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-85) It continued to be an expensive institution to run, particularly when the prison was full, such as during 1691 when numbers were inflated by the campaign against French Protestants and the annual cost of running the Bastille rose to 232,818 livres.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-86)[[G]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-88)

Between 1715 – the year of Louis's death – and 1723, power transferred to the _[Régence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A9gence "Régence")_; the regent, [Philippe d'Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_II,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Philippe II, Duke of Orléans"), maintained the prison but the absolutist rigour of Louis XIV's system began to weaken somewhat.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-89) Although Protestants ceased to be kept in the Bastille, the political uncertainties and plots of the period kept the prison busy and 1,459 were imprisoned there under the Regency, an average of around 182 a year.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-90) During the [Cellamare conspiracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellamare_conspiracy "Cellamare conspiracy"), the alleged enemies of the Regency were imprisoned in the Bastille, including [Marguerite De Launay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_de_Launay,_baronne_de_Staal "Marguerite de Launay, baronne de Staal").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-FunckP73-91) While in the Bastille, de Launay fell in love with a fellow prisoner, the Chevalier de Ménil; she also infamously received an invitation of marriage from the Chevalier de Maisonrouge, the governor's deputy, who had fallen in love with her himself.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-FunckP73-91)

### Reigns of Louis XV and Louis XVI (1723–1789)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Reigns of Louis XV and Louis XVI (1723–1789)")]

#### Architecture and organisation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Architecture and organisation")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Bastille_profile%2C_1750.jpg/500px-Bastille_profile%2C_1750.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_profile,_1750.jpg)

A cross-section of the Bastille viewed from the south in 1750

By the late 18th century, the Bastille had come to separate the more aristocratic quarter of [The Marais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Marais "The Marais") in the old city from the working class district of the faubourg Saint-Antoine that lay beyond the Louis XIV boulevard.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-BNF1-70) The Marais was a fashionable area, frequented by foreign visitors and tourists, but few went beyond the Bastille into the faubourg.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-92) The faubourg was characterised by its built-up, densely populated areas, particularly in the north, and its numerous workshops producing soft furnishings.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-93) Paris as a whole had continued to grow, reaching slightly less than 800,000 inhabitants by the reign of Louis XVI, and many of the residents around the faubourg had migrated to Paris from the countryside relatively recently.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-94) The Bastille had its own street address, being officially known as No. 232, rue Saint-Antoine.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-95)

Structurally, the late-18th century Bastille was not greatly changed from its 14th-century predecessor.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-96) The eight stone towers had gradually acquired individual names: running from the north-east side of the external gate, these were La Chapelle, Trésor, Comté, Bazinière, Bertaudière, Liberté, Puits and Coin.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Chevallier,_p._148-97) La Chapelle contained the Bastille's chapel, decorated with a painting of [Saint Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Peter "Saint Peter") in chains.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-98) Trésor took its name from the reign of Henry IV, when it had contained the royal treasury.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP46-99) The origins of the name of Comté tower are unclear; one theory is that the name refers to the County of Paris.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-100) Bazinière was named after Bertrand de La Bazinière, a royal treasurer who was imprisoned there in 1663.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP46-99) Bertaudière was named after a medieval mason who died building the structure in the 14th century.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP47-101) Liberté tower took its name either from a protest in 1380, when Parisians shouted the phrase outside the castle, or because it was used to house prisoners who had more freedom to walk around the castle than the typical prisoner.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-102) Puits tower contained the [castle well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_well "Castle well"), while Coin formed the corner of the Rue Saint-Antoine.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP47-101)
