### 15th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 15th century")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Bastille_in_Medieval_Paris_Map..png/250px-Bastille_in_Medieval_Paris_Map..png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_in_Medieval_Paris_Map..png)

Parisian defences in 14th century: A – [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre_Palace "Louvre Palace"); B – Palais de Roi; C – Hôtel des Tournelles; D – [Porte Saint-Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porte_Saint-Antoine "Porte Saint-Antoine"); E – Hôtel St Paul; F – the Bastille

During the 15th century, the French kings continued to engage in conflict with the English, [Burgundians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Burgundy "Duchy of Burgundy") and [Armagnacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armagnac_(party) "Armagnac (party)").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-21) The Bastille was strategically vital during the period, both because of its role as a royal fortress and safe-haven inside the capital, and because it controlled a critical route in and out of Paris.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-22) In 1418, for example, the future [Charles VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VII_of_France "Charles VII of France") took refuge in the Bastille during the Burgundian-led "[Massacre of the Armagnacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_coup_d'%C3%A9tat_and_massacres_of_1418 "Paris coup d'état and massacres of 1418")" in Paris, before successfully fleeing the city through the Porte Saint-Antoine.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-23) The Bastille was occasionally used to hold prisoners, including its creator, [Hugues Aubriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugues_Aubriot "Hugues Aubriot"), who was the first person to be imprisoned there. In 1417, in addition to being a royal fortress, it formally became a state prison.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP4-24)[[C]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-26)

Despite the improved Parisian defences, [Henry V of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England "Henry V of England") captured Paris in 1420 and the Bastille was garrisoned by the English for the next sixteen years.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP4-24) Henry V appointed [Thomas Beaufort, Duke of Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Beaufort,_Duke_of_Exeter "Thomas Beaufort, Duke of Exeter"), as the new captain of the Bastille.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP4-24) The English made more use of the Bastille as a prison; in 1430 there was a minor rebellion when some prisoners overpowered a sleeping guard and attempted to seize control of the fortress; this incident includes the first reference to a dedicated gaoler at the Bastille.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-27)

Paris was finally recaptured by Charles VII of France in 1436. When the French king re-entered the city, his enemies in Paris fortified themselves in the Bastille; after a siege, they eventually ran out of food, surrendered and were allowed to leave the city after the payment of a ransom.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-28) The castle remained a key Parisian fortress, but was successfully seized by the Burgundians in 1464, when they convinced royal troops to surrender: once taken, this allowed their faction to make a surprise attack into Paris, almost resulting in the capture of the king.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-29)

The Bastille was being used to hold prisoners once again by the reign of [Louis XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XI "Louis XI"), who began to use it extensively as a state penitentiary.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-30) An early escapee from the Bastille during this period was [Antoine de Chabannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_de_Chabannes "Antoine de Chabannes"), Count of Dammartin and a member of the [League of the Public Weal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_the_Public_Weal "League of the Public Weal"), who was imprisoned by Louis and escaped by boat in 1465.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-31) The captains of the Bastille during this period were primarily officers and royal functionaries; Philippe de [Melun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melun "Melun") was the first captain to receive a salary in 1462, being awarded 1,200 [livres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_livre "French livre") a year.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-32)[[D]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-34) Despite being a state prison, the Bastille retained the other traditional functions of a royal castle, and was used to accommodate visiting dignitaries, hosting some lavish entertainments given by Louis XI and [Francis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_I_of_France "Francis I of France").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-35)

### 16th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 16th century")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Bastille_district_1575.jpg/500px-Bastille_district_1575.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_district_1575.jpg)

A depiction of the Bastille and neighbouring Paris in 1575, showing the new [bastions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion"), the new Porte Saint-Antoine, the [Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_of_Paris?action=edit&redlink=1 "Arsenal of Paris (page does not exist)") complex and the open countryside beyond the city defences

During the 16th century the area around the Bastille developed further. Early modern Paris continued to grow, and by the end of the century it had around 250,000 inhabitants and was one of the most populous cities in Europe, though still largely contained within its old city walls – open countryside remained beyond the Bastille.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-36) The [Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_of_Paris?action=edit&redlink=1 "Arsenal of Paris (page does not exist)"), a large military-industrial complex tasked with the production of cannons and other weapons for the royal armies, was established to the south of the Bastille by Francis I, and substantially expanded under [Charles IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_IX_of_France "Charles IX of France").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-37) An arms depot was later built above the Porte Saint-Antoine, all making the Bastille part of a major military centre.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-38)

During the 1550s, [Henry II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_II_of_France "Henry II of France") became concerned about the possibility of an attack on Paris by England or the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), and strengthened the defences of the Bastille in response.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-39) The southern gateway into the Bastille became the principal entrance to the castle in 1553, the other three gateways being closed.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP4-24) A [bastion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion"), a large earthwork projecting eastwards from the Bastille, was built to provide additional [protective fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suppressive_fire "Suppressive fire") for the Bastille and the Arsenal; the bastion was reached from the fortress across a stone [abutment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abutment "Abutment") using a connecting drawbridge that was installed in the Bastille's Comté tower.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-40) In 1573 the Porte Saint-Antoine was also altered – the drawbridges were replaced with a fixed bridge, and the medieval gatehouse was replaced with a [triumphal arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triumphal_arch "Triumphal arch").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-41)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Callot_view_of_the_Bastille.jpg/250px-Callot_view_of_the_Bastille.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Callot_view_of_the_Bastille.jpg)

The Bastille in 1647, illustrating the bastion, the stone [abutment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abutment "Abutment") linking to the fortress and the new southern entrance built during the 1550s

The Bastille was involved in the numerous [wars of religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion "French Wars of Religion") fought between Protestant and Catholic factions with support from foreign allies during the second half of the 16th century. Religious and political tensions in Paris initially exploded in the [Day of the Barricades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Barricades "Day of the Barricades") on 12 May 1588, when hard-line Catholics rose up in revolt against the relatively moderate [Henry III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_III_of_France "Henry III of France"). After a day's fighting had occurred across the capital, Henry III fled and the Bastille surrendered to [Henry I, Duke of Guise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_I,_Duke_of_Guise "Henry I, Duke of Guise"), the leader of the [Catholic League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_League_(French) "Catholic League (French)"), who appointed Bussy-Leclerc as his new captain.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-42) Henry III responded by having the Duke and his brother murdered later that year, whereupon Bussy-Leclerc used the Bastille as a base to mount a raid on the [Parlement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlement_of_Paris "Parlement of Paris"), arresting the president and other magistrates, whom he suspected of having royalist sympathies, and detaining them in the Bastille.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-43) They were not released until the intervention of [Charles, Duke of Mayenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Mayenne "Charles, Duke of Mayenne"), and the payment of substantial ransoms.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-44) Bussy-Leclerc remained in control of the Bastille until December 1592, when, following further political instability, he was forced to surrender the castle to Charles and flee the city.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-45)

It took [Henry IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_France "Henry IV of France") several years to retake Paris. By the time he succeeded in 1594, the area around the Bastille formed the main stronghold for the Catholic League and their foreign allies, including Spanish and Flemish troops.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-46) The Bastille itself was controlled by a League captain called du Bourg.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-47) Henry entered Paris early on the morning of 23 March, through the Porte-Neuve rather than the Saint-Antoine and seized the capital, including the Arsenal complex that neighboured the Bastille.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-48) The Bastille was now an isolated League stronghold, with the remaining members of the League and their allies clustering around it for safety.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-49) After several days of tension, an agreement was finally reached for this rump element to leave safely, and on 27 March du Bourg surrendered the Bastille and left the city himself.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-50)

### Early 17th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Early 17th century")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Episode_of_the_Fronde_at_the_Faubourg_Saint-Antoine_by_the_Walls_of_the_Bastille.png/250px-Episode_of_the_Fronde_at_the_Faubourg_Saint-Antoine_by_the_Walls_of_the_Bastille.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Episode_of_the_Fronde_at_the_Faubourg_Saint-Antoine_by_the_Walls_of_the_Bastille.png)

A contemporary depiction of the [battle of the Faubourg St Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Faubourg_St_Antoine "Battle of the Faubourg St Antoine") beneath the walls of the Bastille in 1652

The Bastille continued to be used as a prison and a royal fortress under both Henry IV and his son, [Louis XIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIII "Louis XIII"). When Henry clamped down on a Spanish-backed plot among the senior [French nobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_nobility "French nobility") in 1602, for example, he detained the ringleader [Charles de Gontaut, duc de Biron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gontaut,_duc_de_Biron "Charles de Gontaut, duc de Biron"), in the Bastille, and had him executed in the courtyard.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-51) Louis XIII's chief minister, [Cardinal Richelieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Richelieu "Cardinal Richelieu"), is credited with beginning the modern transformation of the Bastille into a more formal organ of the French state, further increasing its structured use as a state prison.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-52) Richelieu broke with Henry IV's tradition of the Bastille's captain being a member of the French aristocracy, typically a [Marshal of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshal_of_France "Marshal of France") such as [François de Bassompierre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_de_Bassompierre "François de Bassompierre"), [Charles d'Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_d'Albert,_duc_de_Luynes "Charles d'Albert, duc de Luynes") or [Nicolas de L'Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_de_L'Hospital "Nicolas de L'Hospital"), and instead appointed [Père Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Leclerc_du_Tremblay "François Leclerc du Tremblay")'s brother to run the facility.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-53)[[E]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-55) The first surviving documentary records of prisoners at the Bastille also date from this period.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-56)

In 1648, the [Fronde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fronde "Fronde") insurrection broke out in Paris, prompted by high taxes, increased food prices and disease.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Munck,_p._212-57) The _Parlement of Paris_, the Regency government of [Anne of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_of_Austria "Anne of Austria") and rebellious noble factions fought for several years to take control of the city and wider power. On 26 August, during the period known as the First Fronde, Anne ordered the arrest of some of the leaders of the Parlement of Paris; violence flared as a result, and the 27 August became known as another [Day of the Barricades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Barricades "Day of the Barricades").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-58) The governor of the Bastille loaded and readied his guns to fire on the [Hôtel de Ville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_de_Ville,_Paris "Hôtel de Ville, Paris"), controlled by the parliament, although the decision was eventually taken not to shoot.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-59) Barricades were erected across the city and the royal government fled in September, leaving a garrison of 22 men behind in the Bastille.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-60) On 11 January 1649, the Fronde decided to take the Bastille, giving the task to Elbeuf, one of their leaders.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-61) Elbeuf's attack required only a token effort: five or six shots were fired at the Bastille, before it promptly surrendered on 13 January.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-62)[Pierre Broussel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Broussel "Pierre Broussel"), one of the Fronde leaders, appointed his son as the governor and the Fronde retained it even after the ceasefire that March.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-63)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Bastille_1649.jpg/500px-Bastille_1649.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_1649.jpg)

The Bastille and the eastern side of Paris in 1649

During the Second Fronde, between 1650 and 1653, [Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis,_Grand_Cond%C3%A9 "Louis, Grand Condé"), the Prince of Condé, controlled much of Paris alongside the Parlement, while Broussel, through his son, continued to control the Bastille. In July 1652, the [Battle of the Faubourg St Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Faubourg_St_Antoine "Battle of the Faubourg St Antoine") took place just outside the Bastille. Condé had sallied out of Paris to prevent the advance of the royalist forces under the command of [Turenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_la_Tour_d'Auvergne,_Vicomte_de_Turenne "Henri de la Tour d'Auvergne, Vicomte de Turenne").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-64) Condé's forces became trapped against the city walls and the Porte Saint-Antoine, which the Parlement refused to open; he was coming under increasingly heavy fire from the Royalist artillery and the situation looked bleak.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-65) In a famous incident, [La Grande Mademoiselle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Marie_Louise_d'Orl%C3%A9ans,_Duchess_of_Montpensier "Anne Marie Louise d'Orléans, Duchess of Montpensier"), the daughter of [Gaston, Duke of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaston,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Gaston, Duke of Orléans"), convinced her father to issue an order for the Parisian forces to act, before she then entered the Bastille and personally ensured that the commander turned the fortress's cannon on Turenne's army, causing significant casualties and enabling Condé's army's safe withdrawal.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-66) Later in 1652, Condé was finally forced to surrender Paris to the royalist forces in October, effectively bringing the Fronde to an end: the Bastille returned to royal control.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Munck,_p._212-57)

### Reign of Louis XIV and the Regency (1661–1723)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Reign of Louis XIV and the Regency (1661–1723)")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Bastille_1715.jpg/500px-Bastille_1715.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_1715.jpg)

The Bastille and Porte Saint-Antoine from the north-east, 1715–19

The area around the Bastille was transformed in the reign of Louis XIV. Paris' growing population reached 400,000 during the period, causing the city to spill out past the Bastille and the old city into the arable farmland beyond, forming more thinly populated _[faubourgs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faubourg "Faubourg")_, or suburbs.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-67) Influenced by the events of the Fronde, Louis XIV rebuilt the area around the Bastille, erecting a new archway at the Porte Saint-Antoine in 1660, and then ten years later pulling down the city walls and their supporting fortifications to replace them with an avenue of trees, later called Louis XIV's boulevard, which passed around the Bastille.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-68) The Bastille's bastion survived the redevelopment, becoming a garden for the use of the prisoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-69)

Louis XIV made extensive use of the Bastille as a prison, with 2,320 individuals being detained there during his reign, approximately 43 a year.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-BNF1-70) Louis used the Bastille to hold not just suspected rebels or plotters but also those who had simply irritated him in some way, such as differing with him on matters of religion.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-71) The typical offences that inmates were accused of were espionage, counterfeiting and embezzlement from the state; a number of financial officials were detained in this way under Louis, most famously including [Nicolas Fouquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Fouquet "Nicolas Fouquet"), his supporters [Henry de Guénegaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_de_Gu%C3%A9negaud "Henry de Guénegaud"), Jeannin and [Lorenzo de Tonti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenzo_de_Tonti "Lorenzo de Tonti").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-72) In 1685 Louis [revoked the Edict of Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Fontainebleau "Edict of Fontainebleau"), which had previously granted various rights to French Protestants; the subsequent royal crackdown was driven by the king's strongly anti-Protestant views.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-73) The Bastille was used to investigate and break up Protestant networks by imprisoning and questioning the more recalcitrant members of the community, in particular upper-class [Calvinists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinist "Calvinist"); some 254 Protestants were imprisoned in the Bastille during Louis's reign.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-74)

By Louis's reign, Bastille prisoners were detained using a _[lettre de cachet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lettre\_de\_cachet "Lettre de cachet")_, a letter under royal seal, issued by the king and countersigned by a minister, ordering a named person to be held.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-TroutP142-75) Louis, closely involved in this aspect of government, personally decided who should be imprisoned at the Bastille.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-BNF1-70) The arrest itself involved an element of ceremony: the individual would be tapped on the shoulder with a white baton and formally detained in the name of the king.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-TroutP143-76) Detention in the Bastille was typically ordered for an indefinite period and there was considerable secrecy over who had been detained and why: the legend of the "Man in the Iron Mask", a mysterious prisoner who finally died in 1703, symbolises this period of the Bastille.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-77) Although in practice many were held at the Bastille as a form of punishment, legally a prisoner in the Bastille was only being detained for preventative or investigative reasons: the prison was not officially supposed to be a punitive measure in its own right.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-TroutP141-78) The average length of imprisonment in the Bastille under Louis XIV was approximately three years.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-LusebrinkP51-79)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Bastille%2C_1734.jpg/250px-Bastille%2C_1734.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille,_1734.jpg)

The Bastille in 1734, showing the Louis XIV boulevard and the growing "[faubourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faubourg "Faubourg")" beyond the Porte Saint-Antoine

Under Louis, only between 20 and 50 prisoners were usually held at the Bastille at any one time, although as many as 111 were held for a short period in 1703.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-TroutP142-75) These prisoners were mainly from the upper classes, and those who could afford to pay for additional luxuries lived in good conditions, wearing their own clothes, living in rooms decorated with tapestries and carpets or taking exercise around the castle garden and along the walls.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-TroutP141-78) By the late 17th century, there was a rather disorganised library for the use of inmates in the Bastille, although its origins remain unclear.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-80)[[F]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-82)

Louis reformed the administrative structure of the Bastille, creating the post of governor, although this post was still often referred to as the captain-governor.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-83) During Louis's reign the policing of marginal groups in Paris was greatly increased: the wider criminal justice system was reformed, controls over printing and publishing extended, new criminal codes were issued and the post of the Parisian [lieutenant general of police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefecture_of_Police "Prefecture of Police") was created in 1667, all of which would enable the Bastille's later role in support of the Parisian police during the 18th century.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-84) By 1711, a 60-strong French military garrison had been established at the Bastille.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-85) It continued to be an expensive institution to run, particularly when the prison was full, such as during 1691 when numbers were inflated by the campaign against French Protestants and the annual cost of running the Bastille rose to 232,818 livres.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-86)[[G]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-88)

Between 1715 – the year of Louis's death – and 1723, power transferred to the _[Régence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A9gence "Régence")_; the regent, [Philippe d'Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_II,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Philippe II, Duke of Orléans"), maintained the prison but the absolutist rigour of Louis XIV's system began to weaken somewhat.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-89) Although Protestants ceased to be kept in the Bastille, the political uncertainties and plots of the period kept the prison busy and 1,459 were imprisoned there under the Regency, an average of around 182 a year.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-90) During the [Cellamare conspiracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellamare_conspiracy "Cellamare conspiracy"), the alleged enemies of the Regency were imprisoned in the Bastille, including [Marguerite De Launay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_de_Launay,_baronne_de_Staal "Marguerite de Launay, baronne de Staal").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-FunckP73-91) While in the Bastille, de Launay fell in love with a fellow prisoner, the Chevalier de Ménil; she also infamously received an invitation of marriage from the Chevalier de Maisonrouge, the governor's deputy, who had fallen in love with her himself.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-FunckP73-91)

### Reigns of Louis XV and Louis XVI (1723–1789)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Reigns of Louis XV and Louis XVI (1723–1789)")]

#### Architecture and organisation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Architecture and organisation")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Bastille_profile%2C_1750.jpg/500px-Bastille_profile%2C_1750.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_profile,_1750.jpg)

A cross-section of the Bastille viewed from the south in 1750

By the late 18th century, the Bastille had come to separate the more aristocratic quarter of [The Marais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Marais "The Marais") in the old city from the working class district of the faubourg Saint-Antoine that lay beyond the Louis XIV boulevard.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-BNF1-70) The Marais was a fashionable area, frequented by foreign visitors and tourists, but few went beyond the Bastille into the faubourg.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-92) The faubourg was characterised by its built-up, densely populated areas, particularly in the north, and its numerous workshops producing soft furnishings.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-93) Paris as a whole had continued to grow, reaching slightly less than 800,000 inhabitants by the reign of Louis XVI, and many of the residents around the faubourg had migrated to Paris from the countryside relatively recently.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-94) The Bastille had its own street address, being officially known as No. 232, rue Saint-Antoine.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-95)

Structurally, the late-18th century Bastille was not greatly changed from its 14th-century predecessor.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-96) The eight stone towers had gradually acquired individual names: running from the north-east side of the external gate, these were La Chapelle, Trésor, Comté, Bazinière, Bertaudière, Liberté, Puits and Coin.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Chevallier,_p._148-97) La Chapelle contained the Bastille's chapel, decorated with a painting of [Saint Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Peter "Saint Peter") in chains.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-98) Trésor took its name from the reign of Henry IV, when it had contained the royal treasury.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP46-99) The origins of the name of Comté tower are unclear; one theory is that the name refers to the County of Paris.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-100) Bazinière was named after Bertrand de La Bazinière, a royal treasurer who was imprisoned there in 1663.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP46-99) Bertaudière was named after a medieval mason who died building the structure in the 14th century.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP47-101) Liberté tower took its name either from a protest in 1380, when Parisians shouted the phrase outside the castle, or because it was used to house prisoners who had more freedom to walk around the castle than the typical prisoner.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-102) Puits tower contained the [castle well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_well "Castle well"), while Coin formed the corner of the Rue Saint-Antoine.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-CoueretP47-101)

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/REVOLUTION_ET_GUERRE.JPG/250px-REVOLUTION_ET_GUERRE.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:REVOLUTION_ET_GUERRE.JPG)

The Bells of the Bastille Clock

The main castle courtyard, accessed through the southern gateway, was 120 feet long by 72 feet wide (37 m by 22 m), and was divided from the smaller northern yard by a three-office wing, built around 1716 and renovated in 1761 in a modern, 18th-century style.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-103) The office wing held the council room that was used for interrogating prisoners, the Bastille's library, and servants' quarters.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-104) The upper stories included rooms for the senior Bastille staff, and chambers for distinguished prisoners.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-105) An elevated building on one side of the courtyard held the Bastille's archives.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-106) A clock was installed by [Antoine de Sartine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_de_Sartine "Antoine de Sartine"), the lieutenant general of police between 1759 and 1774, on the side of the office wing, depicting two chained prisoners.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-107)

New kitchens and baths were built just outside the main gate to the Bastille in 1786.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Chevallier,_p._148-97) The ditch around the Bastille, now largely dry, supported a 36-foot (11 m) high stone wall with a wooden walkway for the use of the guards, known as "la ronde", or the round.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-108) An outer court had grown up around the south-west side of the Bastille, adjacent to the Arsenal. This was open to the public and lined with small shops rented out by the governor for almost 10,000 livres a year, complete with a lodge for the Bastille gatekeeper; it was illuminated at night to light the adjacent street.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-109)

The Bastille was run by the governor, sometimes called the captain-governor, who lived in a 17th-century house alongside the fortress.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-DutrayP136-110) The governor was supported by various officers, in particular his deputy, the _lieutenant de roi_, or lieutenant of the king, who was responsible for general security and the protection of state secrets; the major, responsible for managing the Bastille's financial affairs and the police archives; and the _capitaine des portes_, who ran the entrance to the Bastille.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-DutrayP136-110) Four warders divided up the eight towers between them.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-111) From an administrative perspective, the prison was generally well run during the period.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-DutrayP136-110) These staff were supported by an official surgeon, a chaplain and could, on occasion, call upon the services of a local midwife to assist pregnant prisoners.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-112)[[H]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-114) A small garrison of "[invalides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invalides "Invalides")" was appointed in 1749 to guard the interior and exterior of the fortress; these were retired soldiers and were regarded locally, as [Simon Schama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Schama "Simon Schama") describes, as "amiable layabouts" rather than professional soldiers.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-115)

#### Use of the prison

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Use of the prison")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Convulsionnaires_in_the_Bastille.png/250px-Convulsionnaires_in_the_Bastille.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Convulsionnaires_in_the_Bastille.png)

[Jansenist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jansenism "Jansenism")[convulsionnaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convulsionnaires_of_Saint-M%C3%A9dard "Convulsionnaires of Saint-Médard") exercising in the outer court

The role of the Bastille as a prison changed considerably during the reigns of Louis XV and XVI. One trend was a decline in the number of prisoners sent to the Bastille, with 1,194 imprisoned there during the reign of Louis XV and only 306 under Louis XVI up until the Revolution, annual averages of around 23 and 20 respectively.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-BNF1-70)[[I]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-116) A second trend was a slow shift away from the Bastille's 17th-century role of detaining primarily upper-class prisoners, towards a situation in which the Bastille was essentially a location for imprisoning socially undesirable individuals of all backgrounds – including aristocrats breaking social conventions, criminals, pornographers, thugs – and was used to support police operations, particularly those involving censorship, across Paris.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-117) Despite these changes, the Bastille remained a state prison, subject to special authorities, answering to the monarch of the day and surrounded by a considerable and threatening reputation.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-118)

Under Louis XV, around 250 Catholic [convulsionnaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convulsionnaires_of_Saint-M%C3%A9dard "Convulsionnaires of Saint-Médard"), often called [Jansenists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jansenism "Jansenism"), were detained in the Bastille for their religious beliefs.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-119) Many of these prisoners were women and came from a wider range of social backgrounds than the upper-class Calvinists detained under Louis XIV; historian Monique Cottret argues that the decline of the Bastille's social "mystique" originates from this phase of detentions.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-120) By Louis XVI, the background of those entering the Bastille and the type of offences they were detained over had changed markedly. Between 1774 and 1789, the detentions included 54 people accused of robbery; 31 of involvement in the 1775 Famine Revolt; 11 detained for assault; 62 illegal editors, printers and writers – but relatively few detained over the grander affairs of state.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-LusebrinkP51-79)

Many prisoners still continued to come from the upper classes, particularly in those cases termed _désordres des familles_, or disorders of the family. These cases typically involving members of the aristocracy who had, as historian Richard Andrews notes, "rejected parental authority, disgraced the family reputation, manifested mental derangement, squandered capital or violated professional codes."[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-121) Their families – often their parents, but sometimes husbands and wives taking action against their spouses – could apply for individuals to be detained at one of the royal prisons, resulting in an average imprisonment of between six months and four years.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-122) Such a detention could be preferable to facing a scandal or a public trial over their misdemeanours, and the secrecy that surrounded detention at the Bastille allowed personal and family reputations to be quietly protected.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-123) The Bastille was considered one of the best prisons for an upper-class prisoner to be detained at, because of the standard of the facilities for the wealthy.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-124) In the aftermath of the notorious "[Affair of the Diamond Necklace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affair_of_the_Diamond_Necklace "Affair of the Diamond Necklace")" of 1786, involving Queen [Marie Antoinette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Antoinette "Marie Antoinette") and accusations of fraud, all the eleven suspects were held in the Bastille, significantly increasing the notoriety surrounding the institution.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-125)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Bastille_1789.jpg/500px-Bastille_1789.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_1789.jpg)

The Bastille and the Porte Saint-Antoine, seen from the east

Increasingly, however, the Bastille became part of the system of wider policing in Paris. Although appointed by the king, the governor reported to the lieutenant general of police: the first of these, [Gabriel Nicolas de la Reynie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Nicolas_de_la_Reynie "Gabriel Nicolas de la Reynie"), made only occasional visits to the Bastille, but his successor, [Marquis d'Argenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc-Ren%C3%A9_de_Voyer_de_Paulmy_d'Argenson_(1652%E2%80%931721) "Marc-René de Voyer de Paulmy d'Argenson (1652–1721)"), and subsequent officers used the facility extensively and took a close interest in inspections of the prison.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-126) The lieutenant general reported in turn to the secretary of the _[Maison du Roi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maison\_du\_Roi "Maison du Roi")_, largely responsible for order in the capital; in practice together they controlled the issuing of the _lettres_ in the king's name.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-127) The Bastille was unusual among Parisian prisons in that it acted on behalf of the king – prisoners could therefore be imprisoned secretly, for longer, and without normal judicial processes being applied, making it a useful facility for the police authorities.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-128) The Bastille was a preferred location for holding prisoners who needed extensive questioning or where a case required the analysis of extensive documents.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-129) The Bastille was also used to store the Parisian police archives; public order equipment such as chains and flags; and illegal goods, seized by order of the crown using a version of the _lettre de cachet_, such as banned books and illicit printing presses.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-130)

Throughout this period, but particularly in the middle of the 18th century, the Bastille was used by the police to suppress the trade in illegal and seditious [books in France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Books_in_France "Books in France").[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-BirnP51-131) In the 1750s, 40% of those sent to the Bastille were arrested for their role in manufacturing or dealing in banned material; in the 1760s, the equivalent figure was 35%.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-BirnP51-131)[[J]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-133) Seditious writers were also often held in the Bastille, although many of the more famous writers held in the Bastille during the period were formally imprisoned for more anti-social, rather than strictly political, offences.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-134) In particular, many of those writers detained under Louis XVI were imprisoned for their role in producing illegal pornography, rather than political critiques of the regime.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-LusebrinkP51-79) The writer [Laurent Angliviel de la Beaumelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_Angliviel_de_la_Beaumelle "Laurent Angliviel de la Beaumelle"), the philosopher [André Morellet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Morellet "André Morellet") and the historian [Jean-François Marmontel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Fran%C3%A7ois_Marmontel "Jean-François Marmontel"), for example, were formally detained not for their more obviously political writings, but for libellous remarks or for personal insults against leading members of Parisian society.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-135)

#### Prison regime

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Prison regime")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Bastille_Courtyard_1785.jpg/250px-Bastille_Courtyard_1785.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_Courtyard_1785.jpg)

A sketch of the main courtyard in 1785[[K]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-137)

Contrary to its later image, conditions for prisoners in the Bastille by the mid-18th century were in fact relatively benign, particularly by the standards of other prisons of the time.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-138) The typical prisoner was held in one of the octagonal rooms in the [mid-levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Levels "Mid-Levels") of the towers.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-139) The _calottes_, the rooms just under the roof that formed the upper storey of the Bastille, were considered the least pleasant quarters, being more exposed to the elements and usually either too hot or too cold.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP331-140) The _cachots_, the underground dungeons, had not been used for many years except for holding recaptured escapees.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP331-140) Prisoners' rooms each had a stove or a fireplace, basic furniture, curtains and in most cases a window. A typical criticism of the rooms was that they were shabby and basic rather than uncomfortable.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-141)[[L]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-143) Like the _calottes_, the main courtyard, used for exercise, was often criticised by prisoners as being unpleasant at the height of summer or winter, although the garden in the bastion and the castle walls were also used for recreation.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-144)

The governor received money from the Crown to support the prisoners, with the amount varying on rank: the governor received 19 livres a day for each political prisoner – with [conseiller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Councillor_of_State_(France) "Councillor of State (France)")-grade nobles receiving 15 livres – and, at the other end of the scale, three livres a day for each commoner.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP332-145) Even for the commoners, this sum was around twice the daily wage of a labourer and provided for an adequate diet, while the upper classes ate very well: even critics of the Bastille recounted many excellent meals, often taken with the governor himself.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-146)[[M]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-148) Prisoners who were being punished for misbehaviour, however, could have their diet restricted as a punishment.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-149) The medical treatment provided by the Bastille for prisoners was excellent by the standards of the 18th century; the prison also contained a number of inmates suffering from [mental illnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_illness "Mental illness") and took, by the standards of the day, a very progressive attitude to their care.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-150)

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Bastille_Interior_1785.jpg/250px-Bastille_Interior_1785.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_Interior_1785.jpg)

The council chamber, sketched in 1785

Although potentially dangerous objects and money were confiscated and stored when a prisoner first entered the Bastille, most wealthy prisoners continued to bring in additional luxuries, including pet dogs or cats to control the local vermin.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-151) The [Marquis de Sade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquis_de_Sade "Marquis de Sade"), for example, arrived with an elaborate wardrobe, paintings, tapestries, a selection of perfume, and a collection of 133 books.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP332-145) Card games and billiards were played among the prisoners, and alcohol and tobacco were permitted.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-152) Servants could sometimes accompany their masters into the Bastille, as in the cases of the 1746 detention of the family of [Lord Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Douglas,_14th_Earl_of_Morton "James Douglas, 14th Earl of Morton") and their entire household as British spies: the family's domestic life continued on inside the prison relatively normally.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-153) The prisoners' library had grown during the 18th century, mainly through ad hoc purchases and various confiscations by the Crown, until by 1787 it included 389 volumes.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-154)

The length of time that a typical prisoner was kept at the Bastille continued to decline, and by Louis XVI's reign the average length of detention was only two months.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-LusebrinkP51-79) Prisoners would still be expected to sign a document on their release, promising not to talk about the Bastille or their time within it, but by the 1780s this agreement was frequently broken.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-DutrayP136-110) Prisoners leaving the Bastille could be granted pensions on their release by the Crown, either as a form of compensation or as a way of ensuring future good behaviour – [Voltaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire "Voltaire") was granted 1,200 livres a year, for example, while [Latude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Henri_Latude "Jean Henri Latude") received an annual pension of 400 livres.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-155)[[N]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-157)

#### Criticism and reform

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Criticism and reform")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Bastille_1719.jpg/250px-Bastille_1719.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastille_1719.jpg)

[Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon "Dragon") destroy the Bastille on the title page of Bucquoy's _Die Bastille oder die Hölle der Lebenden_.

During the 18th century, the Bastille was extensively criticised by French writers as a symbol of ministerial [despotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotism "Despotism"), which ultimately resulted in reforms and plans for its abolition.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Reichardt,_p._226-158) The first major criticism was by [Constantin de Renneville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Auguste_Constantin_de_Renneville "René Auguste Constantin de Renneville"), who had been imprisoned in the Bastille for 11 years and published his accounts of the experience in 1715 in his book _L'Inquisition françois_.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-159) Renneville presented a dramatic account of his detention, explaining that, despite being innocent, he had been abused and left to rot in one of the Bastille's _cachot_ dungeons, enchained next to a corpse.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-160) More criticism followed in 1719 when the [Abbé Jean de Bucquoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Albert_d'Archambaud "Jean Albert d'Archambaud"), who had escaped from the Bastille ten years previously, published an account of his adventures from the safety of [Hanover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanover "Hanover"). He gave a similar account to Renneville's and termed the Bastille the "hell of the living".[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-161) Voltaire added to the notorious reputation of the Bastille when he wrote about the case of the "Man in the Iron Mask" in 1751, and later criticised the way he himself was treated while detained in the Bastille, labelling the fortress a "palace of revenge".[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-162)[[O]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-164)

In the 1780s, prison reform became a popular topic for French writers and the Bastille was increasingly condemned as a symbol of arbitrary despotism.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-165) Two authors were particularly influential during that period. The first was [Simon-Nicholas Linguet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Nicholas_Henri_Linguet "Simon-Nicholas Henri Linguet"), who was arrested and detained at the Bastille in 1780, after publishing a critique of [Maréchal Duras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel-F%C3%A9licit%C3%A9_de_Durfort_de_Duras "Emmanuel-Félicité de Durfort de Duras").[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP334-166) After his release, he published his _Mémoires sur la Bastille_ in 1783, a damning critique of the institution.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-167) Linguet criticised, sometimes inaccurately, the physical conditions in which he was kept, but went further by capturing in detail the more psychological effects of the prison regime upon an inmate.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-168)[[P]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-169) Linguet also encouraged Louis XVI to destroy the Bastille, publishing an engraving depicting the king announcing to the prisoners "may you be free and live!", a phrase borrowed from Voltaire.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-Reichardt,_p._226-158)

Linguet's work was followed by another prominent autobiography, Henri Latude's _Le despotisme dévoilé_.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP335-170) Latude was a soldier who was imprisoned in the Bastille following a sequence of complex misadventures, including the sending of a letter bomb to [Madame de Pompadour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madame_de_Pompadour "Madame de Pompadour"), the King's mistress.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP335-170) Latude became famous for managing to escape from the Bastille by means of climbing up the chimney of his cell and then descending the walls with a home-made rope ladder, before being recaptured in Amsterdam by French agents.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-171) Latude was released in 1777, but was rearrested following his publication of a book entitled _Memoirs of Vengeance_.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-172) Pamphlets and magazines publicised Latude's case until he was finally released in 1784.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP338-173) Latude became a popular figure with the [Académie française](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acad%C3%A9mie_fran%C3%A7aise "Académie française"), or French Academy, and his autobiography, although inaccurate in places, did much to reinforce the public perception of the Bastille as a despotic institution.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-174)[[Q]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-176)

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Memoires_sur_la_Bastille.jpg/250px-Memoires_sur_la_Bastille.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Memoires_sur_la_Bastille.jpg)

Linguet's _Mémoires sur la Bastille_, depicting the fictional destruction of the Bastille by Louis XVI

Modern historians of the period, such as Hans-Jürgen Lüsebrink, Simon Schama and [Monique Cottret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monique_Cottret?action=edit&redlink=1 "Monique Cottret (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monique%20Cottret "fr:Monique Cottret")] concur that the actual treatment of prisoners in Bastille was much better than the public impression left through those writings.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-177) Nonetheless, fuelled by the secrecy that still surrounded the Bastille, official as well as public concern about the prison, and the system that supported it, also began to mount, prompting reforms.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-178) As early as 1775, Louis XVI's minister [Malesherbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume-Chr%C3%A9tien_de_Lamoignon_de_Malesherbes "Guillaume-Chrétien de Lamoignon de Malesherbes") had authorised all prisoners to be given newspapers to read, and to be allowed to correspond with their family and friends.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-179) In the 1780s, [Breteuil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auguste_Le_Tonnelier_de_Breteuil "Louis Auguste Le Tonnelier de Breteuil"), the [Secretary of State of the Maison du Roi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_of_the_Maison_du_Roi "Secretary of State of the Maison du Roi"), began a substantial reform of the system of _lettres de cachet_ that sent prisoners to the Bastille: such letters were now required to list the length of time a prisoner would be detained for, and the offence for which they were being held.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-180)

Meanwhile, in 1784, the architect [Alexandre Brogniard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre-Th%C3%A9odore_Brongniart "Alexandre-Théodore Brongniart") proposed that the Bastille be demolished and converted into a circular public space with [colonnades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonnade "Colonnade").[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP338-173) Director-General of Finance [Jacques Necker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Necker "Jacques Necker"), having examined the cost of running the Bastille, amounting to well over 127,000 livres in 1774, proposed closing the institution on the grounds of economy alone.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-181)[[R]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-182) Similarly, Pierre-François de Rivière du Puget,[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-183) the Bastille's _lieutenant de roi_, submitted reports in 1788 suggesting that the authorities close the prison, demolish the fortress and sell the [real estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate "Real estate") off.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-184) In June 1789, the [Académie royale d'architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acad%C3%A9mie_royale_d'architecture "Académie royale d'architecture") proposed a similar scheme to Brogniard's, in which the Bastille would be transformed into an open public area, with a tall column at the centre surrounded by fountains, dedicated to Louis XVI as the "restorer of public freedom".[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP338-173)

The number of prisoners held in the Bastille at any one time declined sharply towards the end of Louis's reign. It contained ten prisoners in September 1782 and, despite a small increase at the beginning of 1788, by July 1789 only seven prisoners remained in custody.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-185) Before any official scheme to close the prison could be enacted, however, disturbances across Paris brought a more violent end to the Bastille.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP338-173)

### The French Revolution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: The French Revolution")]

#### Storming of the Bastille

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Storming of the Bastille")]

Main article: [Storming of the Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storming_of_the_Bastille "Storming of the Bastille")

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Siege_of_the_Bastille_%28Claude_Cholat%29.jpg/250px-Siege_of_the_Bastille_%28Claude_Cholat%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Siege_of_the_Bastille_(Claude_Cholat).jpg)

[An eyewitness painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_the_Bastille_(Cholat) "Siege of the Bastille (Cholat)") of the siege of the Bastille by [Claude Cholat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Cholat "Claude Cholat")[[S]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-187)

By July 1789, [revolutionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution") sentiment was rising in Paris. The [Estates-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estates-General_of_1789 "Estates-General of 1789") was convened in May and members of the Third Estate proclaimed the [Tennis Court Oath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis_Court_Oath "Tennis Court Oath") in June, calling for the king to grant a written constitution. Violence between loyal royal forces, mutinous members of the royal [Gardes Françaises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardes_Fran%C3%A7aises "Gardes Françaises") and local crowds broke out at [Vendôme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vend%C3%B4me "Vendôme") on 12 July, leading to widespread fighting and the withdrawal of royal forces from the centre of Paris.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP327-188) Revolutionary crowds began to arm themselves during 13 July, looting royal stores, gunsmiths and armourers' shops for weapons and gunpowder.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP327-188)

The commander of the Bastille at the time was [Bernard-René de Launay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard-Ren%C3%A9_de_Launay "Bernard-René de Launay"), a conscientious but minor military officer.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP339-189) Tensions surrounding the Bastille had been rising for several weeks. Only seven prisoners remained in the fortress, – the [Marquis de Sade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquis_de_Sade "Marquis de Sade") had been transferred to the [asylum of Charenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charenton_(asylum) "Charenton (asylum)"), after addressing the public from his walks on top of the towers and, once this was forbidden, shouting from the window of his cell.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-190) Sade had claimed that the authorities planned to massacre the prisoners in the castle, which resulted in the governor removing him to an alternative site in early July.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP339-189)

At de Launay's request, an additional force of 32 soldiers from the Swiss Salis-Samade regiment, under the command of [lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant "Lieutenant")[Ludwig von Flüe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Fl%C3%BCe "Ludwig von Flüe"), had been assigned to the Bastille on 7 July, adding to the existing 82 invalides pensioners who formed the regular garrison.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP339-189) De Launay had taken various precautions, raising the drawbridge in the Comté tower and destroying the stone [abutment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abutment "Abutment") that linked the Bastille to its bastion to prevent anyone from gaining access from that side of the fortress.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-191) The shops in the entranceway to the Bastille had been closed and the gates locked. The Bastille was defended by 30 small artillery pieces, but nonetheless, by 14 July de Launay was very concerned about the Bastille's situation.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP339-189) The Bastille, already hugely unpopular with the revolutionary crowds, was now the only remaining royalist stronghold in central Paris, in addition to which he was protecting a recently arrived stock of 250 barrels of valuable gunpowder.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP339-189) To make matters worse, the Bastille had only two days' supply of food and no source of water, making it impossible to withstand a long siege.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP339-189)[[T]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-192)

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Attack_on_Bastille_plan.png/250px-Attack_on_Bastille_plan.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Attack_on_Bastille_plan.png)

A plan of the Bastille and surrounding buildings made immediately after 1789; the red dot marks the perspective of Claude Cholat's painting of the siege.

On the morning of 14 July around 900 people formed outside the Bastille, primarily working-class members of the nearby faubourg Saint-Antoine, but also including some mutinous soldiers and local traders.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-193) The crowd had gathered in an attempt to commandeer the gunpowder stocks known to be held in the Bastille, and at 10:00 am de Launay let in two of their leaders to negotiate with him.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-194) Just after midday, another negotiator was let in to discuss the situation, but no compromise could be reached: the revolutionary representatives now wanted both the guns and the gunpowder in the Bastille to be handed over, but de Launay refused to do so unless he received authorisation from his leadership in [Versailles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Versailles "Palace of Versailles").[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-195) By this point it was clear that the governor lacked the experience or the skills to defuse the situation.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-196)

Just as negotiations were about to recommence at around 1:30 pm, chaos broke out as the impatient and angry crowd stormed the outer courtyard of the Bastille, pushing toward the main gate.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-197) Confused firing broke out in the confined space and chaotic fighting began in earnest between de Launay's forces and the revolutionary crowd as the two sides exchanged fire.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-198) At around 3:30 pm, more mutinous royal forces arrived to reinforce the crowd, bringing with them trained infantry officers and several cannons.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-199) After discovering that their weapons were too light to damage the main walls of the fortress, the revolutionary crowd began to fire their cannons at the wooden gate of the Bastille.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP342-200) By now around 83 of the crowd had been killed and another 15 mortally wounded; only one of the Invalides had been killed in return.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP343-201)

De Launay had limited options: if he allowed the Revolutionaries to destroy his main gate, he would have to turn the cannon directly inside the Bastille's courtyard on the crowds, causing great loss of life and preventing any peaceful resolution of the episode.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP342-200) De Launay could not withstand a long siege, and he was dissuaded by his officers from committing mass suicide by detonating his supplies of powder.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-202) Instead, de Launay attempted to negotiate a surrender, threatening to blow up the Bastille if his demands were not met.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP343-201) In the midst of this attempt, the Bastille's drawbridge suddenly came down and the revolutionary crowd stormed in. Popular myth believes [Stanislas-Marie Maillard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanislas-Marie_Maillard "Stanislas-Marie Maillard") was the first revolutionary to enter the fortress.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-203) De Launay was dragged outside into the streets and killed by the crowd, and three officers and three soldiers were killed during the course of the afternoon by the crowd.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-204) The soldiers of the Swiss Salis-Samade Regiment, however, were not wearing their uniform coats and were mistaken for Bastille prisoners; they were left unharmed by the crowds until they were escorted away by French Guards and other regular soldiers among the attackers.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-205) The valuable powder and guns were seized and a search begun for the other prisoners in the Bastille.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP343-201)

#### Destruction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bastille&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Destruction")]

Within hours of its capture the Bastille began to be used as a powerful symbol to give legitimacy to the revolutionary movement in France.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-206) The faubourg Saint-Antoine's revolutionary reputation was firmly established by their storming of the Bastille and a formal list began to be drawn up of the _vainqueurs_, or "the victorious", who had taken part so as to honour both the fallen and the survivors.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-207) Although the crowd had initially gone to the Bastille searching for gunpowder, historian Simon Schama observes how the captured prison "gave a shape and an image to all the vices against which the Revolution defined itself".[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-ReichardtSchamaP240-208) Indeed, the more despotic and evil the Bastille was portrayed by the pro-revolutionary press, the more necessary and justified the actions of the Revolution became.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-ReichardtSchamaP240-208) Consequently, the late governor, de Launay, was rapidly vilified as a brutal despot.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-209) The fortress itself was described by the revolutionary press as a "place of slavery and horror", containing "machines of death", "grim underground dungeons" and "disgusting caves" where prisoners were left to rot for up to 50 years.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-210)

As a result, in the days after 14 July, the fortress was searched for evidence of torture: old pieces of armour and bits of a printing press were taken out and presented as evidence of elaborate torture equipment.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP345-211) Latude returned to the Bastille, where he was given the rope ladder and equipment with which he had escaped from the prison many years before.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP345-211) The former prison warders escorted visitors around the Bastille in the weeks after its capture, giving colourful accounts of the events in the castle.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP348-212) Stories and pictures about the rescue of the fictional [Count de Lorges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_de_Lorges?action=edit&redlink=1 "Count de Lorges (page does not exist)") – supposedly a mistreated prisoner of the Bastille incarcerated by Louis XV – and the similarly imaginary discovery of the skeleton of the "Man in the Iron Mask" in the dungeons, were widely circulated as fact across Paris.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-213) In the coming months, over 150 [broadside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadside_(printing) "Broadside (printing)") publications used the storming of the Bastille as a theme, while the events formed the basis for a number of theatrical plays.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-214)

Despite a thorough search, the revolutionaries discovered only seven prisoners in the Bastille, rather fewer than had been anticipated.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-215) Of these, only one – de Whyte de Malleville,[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-216) an elderly and white-bearded man – closely resembled the public image of a Bastille prisoner; despite being mentally ill, he was paraded through the streets, where he waved happily to the crowds.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP345-211) Of the remaining six liberated prisoners, four were convicted forgers who quickly vanished into the Paris streets; one was the Count Hubert de Solages, who had been imprisoned on the request of his family for sexual misdemeanours; the sixth was Auguste-Claude Tavernier, who also proved to be mentally ill and, along with Whyte, was in due course reincarcerated in the [Charenton asylum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charenton_(asylum) "Charenton (asylum)").[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaLusebrinkP345-217)[[U]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-218)[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-219)

At first the revolutionary movement was uncertain whether to destroy the prison, to reoccupy it as a fortress with members of the volunteer guard militia, or to preserve it intact as a permanent revolutionary monument.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-220) The revolutionary leader [Mirabeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honor%C3%A9_Gabriel_Riqueti,_comte_de_Mirabeau "Honoré Gabriel Riqueti, comte de Mirabeau") eventually settled the matter by symbolically starting the destruction of the battlements himself, after which a panel of five experts was appointed by the Permanent Committee of the Hôtel de Ville to manage the demolition of the castle.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP348-212)[[V]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-222) One of these experts was [Pierre-François Palloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-Fran%C3%A7ois_Palloy "Pierre-François Palloy"), a bourgeois entrepreneur who claimed vainqueur status for his role during the taking of the Bastille, and he rapidly assumed control over the entire process.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-223) Palloy's team worked quickly and by November most of the fortress had been destroyed.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP349-224)

The ruins of the Bastille rapidly became iconic across France.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP345-211) Palloy had an altar set up on the site in February 1790, formed out of iron chains and restraints from the prison.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP349-224) Old bones, probably of 15th century soldiers, were discovered during the clearance work in April and, presented as the skeletons of former prisoners, were exhumed and ceremonially reburied in Saint-Paul's cemetery.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP350-225) In the summer, a huge ball was held by Palloy on the site for the [National Guardsmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Guard_(France) "National Guard (France)") visiting Paris for the 14 July celebrations.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP350-225) A memorabilia industry surrounding the fall of the Bastille was already flourishing and as the work on the demolition project finally dried up, Palloy started producing and selling memorabilia of the Bastille.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-226)[[W]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-228) Palloy's products, which he called "relics of freedom", celebrated the national unity that the events of July 1789 had generated across all classes of French citizenry, and included a very wide range of items.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-SchamaP351-229)[[X]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-230) Palloy also sent models of the Bastille, carved from the fortress's stones, as gifts to the French provinces at his own expense to spread the revolutionary message.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-231) In 1793 a large revolutionary fountain featuring a statue of [Isis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isis "Isis") was built on the former site of the fortress, which became known as the [Place de la Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_de_la_Bastille "Place de la Bastille").[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille#cite_note-232)
